questions.explanation: The lesson is precise about what counts as evidence: a second tenant is not the same trigger as a second LLM provider requirement — the `org_id` seam pays off with Globex, but the plugin architecture still has no real justification.

options.optionText: Because Globex is a smaller company than Acme and has fewer requirements overall
Because Globex still uses the same single LLM provider Acme does — a second tenant existing is not the same evidence as a second LLM provider being an actual requirement
Because plugin architectures are technically impossible to add once a second tenant exists
Because Meridian's product lead has permanently withdrawn the original request

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson argue that a server-state library like TanStack Query is more than just "less code" compared to hand-rolled `useEffect` fetching for an FDE app with many data-driven components?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is about bug surface area, not raw code volume — fewer hand-written fetch effects means fewer places to reintroduce the exact stale-closure bug Module 3 demonstrated.

options.optionText: It collapses loading, error, staleness, cancellation, and optimistic-update logic into one declarative call, reducing the number of places the same stale-closure class of bug can be reintroduced by each new component
It removes the need for TypeScript entirely in any component that fetches data
It eliminates all network requests by caching data permanently regardless of changes on the server
It is required by React itself for any component that fetches data from an API

questions.questionText: In the scenario, what happens when a reviewer edits a clause's `liabilityCapUsd` value and the resulting PATCH request fails?
questions.explanation: This is the specific behavior the `useMutation` optimistic-update pattern provides: an immediate UI update paired with an automatic rollback if the underlying request does not succeed.

options.optionText: The row silently keeps displaying the new value even though the change was never saved
The optimistic update, which showed the new value immediately, rolls back automatically to the previous value once the mutation reports failure
The entire review queue becomes unresponsive until the page is manually refreshed
The extraction status for the clause is permanently set to `failed`

questions.questionText: In the scenario, a teammate later adds a fourth state, `needs_review`, to `ExtractionResult`. What is the concrete effect on `ClauseCell`'s existing `switch` statement?
questions.explanation: This is the exhaustiveness guarantee made concrete: adding a new union member surfaces every switch that needs updating as a compile error, not a silent runtime gap.

options.optionText: The switch continues to compile and silently renders nothing for the new state until someone notices in production
The switch fails to compile until the new `needs_review` case is explicitly handled, catching the gap before it reaches a reviewer
React automatically generates a default UI for any unhandled discriminated union case
The application crashes at runtime the first time a `needs_review` result is fetched, with no compile-time warning

questions.questionText: Why does `useQuery(['clauses', orgId, contractId], fetchClauses)` avoid re-fetching when a reviewer switches back to a contract they viewed a moment ago?
questions.explanation: The cache key is what makes deduplication and reuse possible — identical keys reuse cached data, distinct keys trigger a fresh fetch.

options.optionText: TanStack Query permanently disables re-fetching after the very first request for any query key
The cache key (`orgId`, `contractId`) lets already-fetched data for that exact key be reused directly from cache instead of triggering a duplicate request
The browser's own HTTP cache is solely responsible for this behavior, unrelated to the query key
Switching contracts never actually changes which data needs to be displayed

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why does a reviewer entering a negative liability cap get rejected the same way whether they use the edit form or a request is sent directly to the mutation?
questions.explanation: This is the practical payoff of a single shared schema — one rule enforced consistently, rather than two separately maintained checks that could disagree.

options.optionText: React automatically blocks all negative numeric inputs across every form by default

Both the form's validation and the mutation's expected type derive from the same Zod schema, so the same validation rule applies regardless of entry point instead of living in two independently maintained places
Negative numbers are rejected by the browser before any JavaScript runs
The backend API silently converts negative values to zero rather than rejecting them

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, when adding pagination or list virtualization for a contract with thousands of extracted clauses, what does the lesson imply is reused unchanged versus what needs genuinely new code?
questions.explanation: The question tests whether the learner understands the actual scope of the change — the caching layer's behavior does not need to change, only how much and which data is requested and rendered at once.

options.optionText: `useQuery`'s caching, deduplication, and staleness behavior is reused as-is; the genuinely new work is rendering only the visible subset of rows and requesting data in pages rather than all at once
Every part of the existing data-fetching layer must be rewritten from scratch for virtualization to work at all
TypeScript's discriminated union types stop functioning correctly once virtualization is introduced
Virtualization eliminates the need for a cache key entirely, since only visible rows are ever fetched

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist the `BYPASSRLS` attribute be reserved for a separate, narrowly-scoped role, never the application's own runtime role?
questions.explanation: The lesson frames this as a single point of failure — one misconfigured connection carrying `BYPASSRLS` defeats database-layer enforcement entirely, which is why it must stay isolated to genuine admin/migration use.

options.optionText: `BYPASSRLS` is a deprecated Postgres feature no longer supported in current versions
Granting `BYPASSRLS` to the application's runtime role undoes the entire point of database-layer enforcement — any connection using that role could return cross-tenant data regardless of the policy
`BYPASSRLS` only affects INSERT statements, so it is irrelevant to read-path tenant isolation
Postgres requires every migration tool to use a role with `BYPASSRLS`, making it unavoidable in practice

questions.questionText: What specific defect does the lesson describe when a worker sets `app.current_org_id` once at worker startup rather than per job?
questions.explanation: This is the exact pooled-connection defect class the lesson names — stale session context from a previous job silently applies to the next job's queries if not explicitly re-set.

options.optionText: The worker crashes immediately on startup and cannot process any jobs
If the connection is reused across jobs for different tenants without re-issuing `SET LOCAL`, a job for one tenant can silently run its queries under a previous job's stale tenant context
Extraction jobs run correctly, but noticeably slower than if the context were set per job
RLS policies stop being enforced entirely once a worker process has been running for more than one job

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson recommend per-tenant queue routing over a single shared FIFO queue for a multi-tenant background worker pool?
questions.explanation: The noisy-neighbor risk is specifically about shared capacity and ordering — a stuck tenant's retries occupy the queue position and worker time that unrelated tenants' quick jobs would otherwise use.

options.optionText: A single shared queue is technically incapable of processing more than one job at a time
One tenant's malformed input triggering repeated retries can occupy worker capacity and queue position, starving every other tenant's quick, legitimate jobs behind it
Celery does not support a single shared queue under any configuration
Per-tenant queues eliminate the need for idempotency keys entirely

questions.questionText: Why is an idempotency key built only from an event ID insufficient in a multi-tenant background job system?
questions.explanation: The specific risk is a cross-tenant identifier collision, which is exactly why the key must be scoped `(org_id, event_id)` rather than the event ID alone.

options.optionText: Event IDs are always too short to be useful as a database key

Two different tenants' independent systems can plausibly generate the same raw identifier, so an event-ID-only key risks one tenant's job silently colliding with, and being dropped or overwritten by, another tenant's job
Idempotency keys are unnecessary once RLS is correctly enforced
Event IDs change every time a job is retried, making them unusable for idempotency in any system

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why did Acme's simple, well-formed uploads end up waiting 40 minutes behind Globex's malformed PDF?
questions.explanation: This is the noisy-neighbor mechanism made concrete — shared queue capacity, not any per-tenant technical block, is what caused Acme's unrelated jobs to wait.

options.optionText: Acme's own contracts were themselves malformed in a similar way

Both tenants' extraction jobs shared a single Celery queue, so Globex's job retrying repeatedly occupied queue position and worker capacity that Acme's quick jobs needed, with no per-tenant isolation to prevent it
RLS policies blocked Acme's jobs from running until Globex's issue was resolved
Acme's worker process had crashed independently of Globex's issue

questions.questionText: What specific defect did the code review catch in the scenario, separate from the noisy-neighbor issue?
questions.explanation: This is the per-job session-context defect from Concepts Covered, made concrete in the scenario as a real code-review catch rather than a hypothetical.

options.optionText: The worker was missing an RLS policy on the `contracts` table entirely

The worker set `app.current_org_id` once at process startup instead of per job, meaning a Globex job processed right after an Acme job on a reused connection could silently query Acme's data under Globex's tenant context if `SET LOCAL` weren't re-issued
The Celery queue name was misspelled in the routing configuration
The idempotency key was missing the event ID component entirely

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, why might per-tenant queue routing alone still be insufficient once a third, unusually high-volume tenant joins?
questions.explanation: Per-tenant queues solve isolation of ordering, but not overall capacity fairness — a large tenant's own queue can still consume a disproportionate share of shared worker capacity without an added concurrency limit.

options.optionText: Per-tenant queues stop working correctly once more than two tenants exist

A single large tenant's own dedicated queue could still monopolize overall worker capacity across the pool, so a per-tenant concurrency limit is needed on top of queue routing to keep that tenant's volume from crowding out others
Per-tenant queues are only compatible with exactly two tenants by design
Idempotency keys need to be redesigned for a third tenant to function

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist OCR error and LLM hallucination need distinct mitigations rather than one generic response?
questions.explanation: Each failure mode has a distinct point of intervention — OCR confidence gating happens before extraction, while grounding checks happen after — so conflating them into one fix leaves a gap.

options.optionText: OCR error and hallucination are actually the same underlying problem described with two different names

OCR error is mitigated by routing low-confidence pages to human-first review before extraction even runs, while hallucination is mitigated by a grounding check on the extraction's own output — treating them as one problem would leave one of the two failure modes unaddressed
OCR error only affects scanned documents, so it can be ignored entirely for any text-native PDF pipeline
Hallucination cannot occur in an extraction pipeline that uses structured JSON output

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson validate the LLM's extraction output against the shared schema on the server, rather than letting a malformed extraction reach the review-queue frontend?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is about where a failure surfaces, not raw execution speed — catching a shape mismatch server-side prevents it from becoming a frontend crash discovered live.

options.optionText: Server-side validation is always faster to execute than client-side validation
A malformed extraction should fail loudly at the point it's produced instead of reaching the frontend as an unexpected shape that crashes a component built for a rigid, fixed contract
The frontend has no ability to display any error state under any circumstances
Schema validation is only possible on a server, never in a browser

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why was the `$500,000` liability-cap extraction flagged as ungrounded instead of entering Acme's review queue as a high-confidence value?
questions.explanation: The scenario is a direct illustration of the grounding check working as designed — the claimed value had no literal basis in the actual source text, so it was rejected rather than trusted.

options.optionText: The LLM itself reported low confidence in the value, which triggered the flag automatically
The grounding check found no literal match for "$500,000" anywhere on page 23's actual OCR'd text, since the real source text was digit-garbled and did not contain that exact figure
Acme's contract review policy requires every liability-cap value to be manually flagged regardless of extraction quality
The extraction pipeline does not support dollar-figure fields at all

questions.questionText: What does the scenario's flagged extraction actually route to, and what does the reviewer receive to resolve it?
questions.explanation: The design specifically gives the reviewer the source material (OCR text and the actual scan) rather than asking them to trust the pipeline's own uncertain output.

options.optionText: The extraction is silently discarded with no notification to any reviewer
It routes to a mandatory human review lane, with the low-confidence OCR page and the original scanned image attached, so the reviewer can resolve the ambiguity by looking directly at the scan
The system automatically substitutes a default liability-cap value of zero
The extraction is re-run automatically with a different LLM model until it passes the grounding check

questions.questionText: What does Practice Loop step 3 — counting how many of ten scanned pages fail versus pass the grounding check — actually establish?
questions.explanation: This is a diagnostic step in the lesson's established pattern: it converts an assumed error rate into a measured one, which is what actually informs whether the human-review lane's capacity is sized correctly.

options.optionText: Whether the extraction prompt is syntactically valid JSON
The pipeline's actual OCR error rate against real scanned pages, which the pipeline's design needs to be built around, rather than an assumed or guessed rate
Whether the ten pages belong to the same tenant or different tenants
The total dollar value of all liability caps extracted across the ten pages

questions.questionText: Why does Practice Loop step 5 ask the learner to confirm grounding-check failures are real issues, not false positives from an overly strict literal-match check?
questions.explanation: An overly strict match tolerance trades one failure mode (missed hallucinations) for another (unnecessary human review load on correct extractions) — step 5 exists to catch that trade-off going too far in the strict direction.

options.optionText: A grounding check that is too strict (rejecting minor whitespace or punctuation differences as non-matches) would route genuinely correct extractions into human review unnecessarily, undermining the pipeline's usefulness even though it is technically safe
False positives are impossible once a grounding check has been implemented correctly
This step exists only to satisfy a compliance requirement unrelated to the pipeline's actual accuracy
The grounding check cannot produce false positives, only false negatives

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what needs to change about the `evidence_quote`/`source_page` design for a liability clause that spans pages 23 and 24?
questions.explanation: The single-page assumption baked into the original design breaks for a clause split across pages — the citation and the grounding check both need to extend to a page range for the same verification logic to still hold.

options.optionText: Nothing — the existing single-page citation design already handles multi-page clauses correctly
The citation needs to reference a page range rather than a single page number, since the grounding check's literal-match comparison must now search across both pages' OCR'd text instead of just one
Multi-page clauses should be excluded from extraction entirely, since they cannot be verified
The evidence_quote field should be removed entirely for any clause spanning more than one page

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson's recommended build order put a hardcoded extraction stub before the real OCR-and-grounded-extraction pipeline?
questions.explanation: The stub's purpose is unblocking parallel frontend work against realistic data, which is why it is deliberately throwaway rather than kept — unlike the RLS seam, which is kept from day one.

options.optionText: The real extraction pipeline is technically impossible to build without a stub existing first
The stub unblocks the review-queue frontend from being built and tested against realistic-shaped data without waiting on the real extraction pipeline, which takes longer to build correctly
Stubs are required by the discovery module's non-goals discipline for every FDE engagement
The real extraction pipeline cannot produce data in the same shape the stub does

questions.questionText: What distinguishes the extraction stub (deliberately throwaway) from the `org_id` column and RLS policy (kept from the first migration), per the lesson's use of the earlier architecture lesson's framework?
questions.explanation: This connects lesson 1's seam-versus-generality distinction directly to this build's real sequencing choices — one decision is cheap to discard, the other is expensive to add later, and the build order treats them accordingly.

options.optionText: There is no meaningful distinction; both should ideally be discarded once the real pipeline exists

The stub exists only to unblock parallel work and is cheap to discard once its purpose is served, while the `org_id` column is the cheap-now, expensive-to-retrofit-later seam that must be kept from day one to avoid a costly migration and leak risk
The `org_id` column should also be discarded once a second tenant onboards, since it was only needed for the pilot
The stub and the `org_id` column serve identical purposes and are interchangeable in the build sequence

questions.questionText: Why does the build order defer per-tenant Celery queue routing until Globex actually onboards, rather than building it alongside the first version of the extraction worker?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the lesson's build-order logic — deferring a feature until there is a real, evidenced need to validate it against, not because it's technically infeasible earlier.

options.optionText: Per-tenant queue routing is technically impossible to implement before a second tenant's data exists in the database

Building queue routing against a single tenant has nothing real to validate it against — the noisy-neighbor problem it solves only becomes real, and testable, once a second tenant's jobs actually share worker capacity
Celery does not support queue routing under any circumstances
Acme explicitly requested that queue routing be delayed as part of the pilot contract

questions.questionText: What specific gap did the pre-launch review of all three RLS entry points catch in the scenario?
questions.explanation: This is the exact gap the "three entry points" claim in Concepts Covered predicts — two boundaries correct, one silently missed, inherited from code that predates the multi-tenant requirement.

options.optionText: The upload handler was missing the `org_id` column on the `contracts` table entirely

The Celery extraction task, copied from an earlier single-tenant prototype, never had the `SET LOCAL app.current_org_id` line added, unlike the upload handler and export endpoint, which both correctly set it
The React review queue was displaying clauses from the wrong tenant on every page load
The export endpoint was exporting clauses before they had been approved by a reviewer

questions.questionText: Why did the missing `SET LOCAL` line in the Celery extraction task produce no visible symptom before the pre-launch review caught it?
questions.explanation: This is exactly why the audit had to be deliberate rather than incidental — a single-tenant system cannot organically surface a cross-tenant enforcement gap through normal use.

options.optionText: With only Acme's data in the system, there was no second tenant's data for a missing tenant-context enforcement to leak into or from, so the gap was invisible until a real cross-tenant scenario existed to expose it
The gap was cosmetic and never actually affected query results, regardless of how many tenants existed
Postgres automatically prevents any query from running without a session variable set, masking the bug
The review queue's polling interval was too slow to display the resulting incorrect data

questions.questionText: What does Practice Loop step 5 (measuring true end-to-end latency and comparing it to the polling interval) actually establish?
questions.explanation: This step converts the "polling is fine at pilot scale" claim from an assumption into something checked against a real measured number, consistent with the lesson's broader insistence on diagnostic steps over assertions.

options.optionText: The exact dollar cost of running the extraction pipeline per contract

Whether the five-second polling interval is still an acceptable user experience given the real, measured latency of the full pipeline, rather than an assumption that polling is fine without ever checking against real numbers
Whether the RLS policy on the `contracts` table is correctly configured
How many concurrent reviewers the system can support at once

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what kind of evidence would justify replacing polling with a WebSocket push notification, rather than building it preemptively?
questions.explanation: This is the same evidenced-need discipline the lesson applies throughout — the upgrade is justified by a real, demonstrated pain point, not by the technology sounding more sophisticated.

options.optionText: A stakeholder's general preference for more modern-sounding technology
A concrete load or customer-feedback threshold, such as multiple concurrent reviewers actively waiting on the same in-flight extraction, where polling's latency becomes a genuinely felt problem
WebSockets should always replace polling as soon as the codebase is stable enough to support the change
The five-second polling interval being technically possible to reduce further

questions.questionText: How does the lesson connect the OpenAPI spec discipline to the earlier frontend lesson's shared Zod schema?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly draws this parallel: single-source-of-truth discipline against drift, applied at a different boundary (external API) than lesson 2's internal form/type boundary.

options.optionText: OpenAPI specs and Zod schemas are literally the same technology used interchangeably

Both apply the same underlying discipline — a single source of truth that generates both the type/validation and the documentation/client, so the two can never silently disagree — just applied to an external API contract here instead of an internal frontend/backend one
The connection is purely coincidental and carries no shared underlying principle
Zod schemas are only usable for external APIs, never for internal frontend forms

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say versioning and a deprecation window matter specifically for an external-facing API, in a way that matters less for a purely internal one?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is about coordination — an internal team can coordinate a deploy directly, while an external integrator has no such coordination channel and needs advance warning instead.

options.optionText: External APIs are technically incapable of being versioned using the same mechanisms as internal ones

An external integrator cannot redeploy their own code on the FDE's schedule, so a breaking change with no warning becomes a production incident on a system the FDE doesn't control and may not even find out about until a support ticket arrives
Internal APIs never change once they are first deployed, unlike external ones
Deprecation windows are a purely cosmetic convention with no practical effect on integrators

questions.questionText: Why did Acme's integration engineer's retry logic hammer the export endpoint for six hours in the scenario?
questions.explanation: The root cause is the undifferentiated 500 response, exactly the problem structured, machine-parseable error codes are designed to fix.

options.optionText: The integration engineer's code had a bug entirely unrelated to the API's error responses

The endpoint returned a bare HTTP 500 with a generic message for both a transient, safely-retryable database hiccup and a permanently malformed request, so the integrator's blanket retry-on-500 logic could not distinguish the two and kept retrying a request that would never succeed
Meridian's servers were experiencing an unrelated outage during that six-hour window
The `/v1/` version prefix had not yet been added to the endpoint at the time

questions.questionText: What did the FDE's fix specifically give Acme's integration engineer, whom the FDE may never speak with directly again after the incident?
questions.explanation: The fix is specifically about self-service — giving the integrator everything needed to build correct code independently, since ongoing direct FDE involvement doesn't scale.

options.optionText: A promise that the export endpoint would never return an error response again

An OpenAPI spec, a structured retryable-vs-not error shape, and a documented deprecation policy — everything needed to build correct, self-correcting integration code without another support call or incident
Direct, ongoing access to the FDE's personal contact information for future troubleshooting
A completely different API endpoint replacing the original export functionality

questions.questionText: Why does Practice Loop step 3 ask the learner to count every genuinely distinct error condition the endpoint can return, rather than stopping once the two conditions from the incident are covered?
questions.explanation: The diagnostic guards against fixing only the specific incident that happened rather than the general class of problem — a narrow fix leaves other undifferentiated error conditions still capable of causing the same kind of incident.

options.optionText: A structured error shape that only covers the specific conditions from one past incident, rather than the endpoint's full range of possible failures, would leave other real error conditions still undifferentiated and vulnerable to the same class of problem
OpenAPI specifications technically require documenting an exact fixed number of error conditions
This step is purely a documentation exercise with no bearing on the integrator's actual retry behavior
Every API must have exactly as many error codes as it has endpoints

questions.questionText: Why does the Suggested Extension add a sandbox or test-mode API key with realistic sample data, rather than having Acme's engineer integrate directly against real tenant data from the start?
questions.explanation: The sandbox key extends the same self-serve philosophy — letting the integrator work independently and safely before real data or a live conversation with the FDE is required.

options.optionText: Real tenant data is technically incompatible with the export API's response format

It lets the integrator build and test their integration independently before being granted access to real, sensitive tenant data — extending the same self-serve, don't-require-a-live-conversation principle the rest of the lesson establishes
Sandbox keys are a regulatory requirement for every enterprise API regardless of data sensitivity
A sandbox key removes the need for the OpenAPI spec entirely

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say a connector that treats every 401 response as a hard failure will fail constantly under normal conditions, not just during an outage?
questions.explanation: Token expiry is routine, not exceptional, so a connector needs a bounded refresh-and-retry step built in — the same "one bounded correction attempt, then a deterministic failure" shape lesson 1 used for schema errors, applied here to expired credentials.

options.optionText: A 401 always indicates the third-party API itself is down

Access tokens are short-lived by design, so a 401 from an expired token is an expected, routine event; a connector needs to refresh the token once and retry before treating the call as failed, the same one-retry discipline lesson 1 applied to a malformed tool call
OAuth2 does not actually support token refresh for server-to-server integrations
A hard failure on 401 is the correct behavior and should never be retried

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson prefer a client-side token-bucket limiter over simply firing requests and backing off after receiving a 429?
questions.explanation: Proactive throttling avoids the cost of ever hitting the limit in the first place — a wasted request and possible temporary block — while reactive backoff is only a recovery mechanism for when a limit has already been exceeded.

options.optionText: Token-bucket limiters are required by the OAuth2 specification

Firing requests at whatever rate the caller allows and only reacting to a 429 wastes a request, adds latency, and risks tripping a temporary block, whereas proactive throttling stays under the documented ceiling before ever triggering a rate-limit response
A 429 response is never actually returned by a well-behaved API
Reactive backoff cannot be implemented without a connector abstraction layer

questions.questionText: Per the lesson, what should actually determine whether a connector uses a webhook or polling to detect a change in a source system?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly reuses lesson 6's freshness-requirement framework rather than introducing a new decision rule — the right choice depends on how quickly a change actually needs to be seen, not on which pattern sounds more advanced.

options.optionText: Whichever pattern is more technically sophisticated should always be preferred
The system's actual freshness requirement — the same question lesson 6's batch-versus-event-driven framework already taught how to ask, not a default preference for one pattern
Polling should always be chosen because it requires no public endpoint
Webhooks should always be chosen because they guarantee exactly-once delivery

questions.questionText: Why does Fenwick's webhook receiving handler check each event's delivery ID against a dedup cache before processing it?
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery is a real, documented guarantee (not exactly-once), so a legitimate duplicate delivery is an expected event the handler must tolerate, not an anomaly.

options.optionText: Zendesk's webhook delivery is guaranteed exactly-once, so this check is only a defensive precaution with no real basis

Zendesk's webhook delivery guarantees at-least-once, meaning the same event can legitimately arrive twice; without a dedup check, a duplicate delivery would trigger the orchestrator a second time for a ticket that only actually changed once
The dedup check exists to detect and reject malicious webhook payloads
Dedup checks are only necessary for polling-based integrations, never webhooks

questions.questionText: Why does the `update_account_note` tool generate an idempotency key from a hash of the ticket ID and note content, rather than relying on the caller to simply not retry a timed-out call?
questions.explanation: This is exactly the ambiguity a timeout creates — the caller cannot distinguish "the write failed" from "the write succeeded but the response was lost," so idempotency is the only safe way to make a retry harmless.

options.optionText: Salesforce rejects any write that lacks an idempotency key, regardless of retry behavior

A write can time out from the caller's perspective while having already succeeded on Salesforce's side; a naive retry without an idempotency key could post the same note twice, so the key lets Salesforce's bulk API deduplicate a retried write against the one that already landed
Idempotency keys are only relevant for reads, never for writes
The ticket ID alone is always sufficient to prevent any duplicate note

questions.questionText: What does the lesson say a connector abstraction layer (a shared `Connector` interface with system-specific implementations) accomplishes?
questions.explanation: The connector layer's value is centralizing genuinely system-specific mechanics in one place, so the tool and MCP-server layers built on top of it don't each need to reimplement the same auth, pagination, and retry logic.

options.optionText: It replaces the need for OAuth authentication entirely

It keeps system-specific plumbing — OAuth refresh, pagination, rate-limit backoff, idempotent writes — in exactly one place per system, instead of scattered across every tool handler and MCP server that happens to touch that system
It eliminates the need for any rate-limit handling
It is only useful once a system has more than one MCP server built for it

questions.questionText: How does the connector abstraction layer from this lesson relate to the MCP servers introduced in lesson 4?
questions.explanation: The two layers are complementary, not competing: the connector owns raw system-specific plumbing, while the MCP server built on top of it owns the resources/tools/prompts primitives and per-client access scoping lesson 4 introduced.

options.optionText: The connector layer replaces the need for MCP servers entirely

The connector layer sits underneath MCP servers — an MCP server's tool handler calls into a connector to actually talk to Salesforce or Zendesk, rather than reimplementing OAuth and pagination itself, extending lesson 4's separation-of-concerns argument one abstraction layer deeper
MCP servers and connectors solve completely unrelated problems with no architectural relationship
A connector must be rebuilt separately for every MCP server that uses it

questions.questionText: Why can a partial failure (the Ledger write succeeding while the Salesforce case update times out) leave two systems permanently disagreeing, with no automatic rollback?
questions.explanation: The absence of a cross-system transaction is exactly why a partial failure needs deliberate reconciliation logic — nothing in either system's own guarantees will notice or fix the mismatch on its own.

options.optionText: Ledger and Salesforce both automatically detect and correct any inconsistency between them

There is no cross-system transaction spanning Ledger and Salesforce the way a database transaction spans tables in one database — when the second write fails, nothing automatically undoes the first, so the integration code itself has to notice and reconcile the resulting inconsistency
Partial failures only occur when a connector's OAuth token has expired
Salesforce writes are always processed before Ledger writes, so this scenario cannot occur

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say schema drift can appear at any time with no deploy of Fenwick's own code to blame it on?
questions.explanation: This is exactly what makes schema drift distinct from most production bugs — its root cause is entirely outside Fenwick's own deploy timeline, which is why an inbound validation layer, not just careful code review, is the practical defense.

options.optionText: Schema drift is always caused by a bug in the connector's own retry logic

A third-party API can silently add, rename, or change a field's semantics without a version bump, and because the third party — not Fenwick — controls that timeline, the connector's field-mapping code can break at any moment the third party changes its shape, independent of anything Fenwick deployed
Schema drift can only occur immediately after Fenwick deploys a new version of its own connector
Third-party APIs are contractually required to give 90 days' notice before any schema change

questions.questionText: What specific advantage does propagating one trace ID across the webhook-to-orchestrator-to-Salesforce-to-Ledger path give an FDE debugging one ticket's outcome, compared to separate per-system logs?
questions.explanation: The value is purely in visibility: a single trace ID turns four scattered, independently-timestamped log entries into one connected view of a single business event's full path.

options.optionText: It eliminates the need for any logging inside the individual systems themselves

It lets the FDE pull one connected timeline showing the webhook receipt, dispatch, and both downstream calls, instead of manually correlating separately-timestamped log entries across four different systems
It automatically fixes any bug found during the investigation

questions.questionText: Why did the twenty-two-minute outage happen in the scenario, given that the connection-pool fix had already been identified and merged?

options.optionText: The fix itself was incorrect and did not actually address the connection-pool issue

questions.questionText: What did the customer-facing RCA sent to Globex deliberately omit, per the scenario, while still being fully accurate about what happened?
questions.explanation: The RCA stayed accurate on every customer-relevant fact while omitting internal implementation detail that wouldn't change the customer's ability to evaluate the incident or trust the fix.

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what's different about the communication Meridian should send Acme, who wasn't actually affected by the outage but asks whether the same issue could hit them?

questions.questionText: Per the lesson's evidence-over-assertion discipline, what does it actually take for the checklist item "RLS coverage audited" to be marked complete?

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist the go-live sign-off meeting is a real event rather than a formality?

questions.questionText: Why did the scenario's security category require Globex's own security team, not just Meridian's, to confirm the BYOK cross-account grant functions as designed?

questions.questionText: What does the scenario's specific runbook entry ("connection pool exhaustion under peak load — see incident RCA-2026-08...") actually give Meridian's platform team?

A directly actionable, citable precedent — the next time a similar symptom appears, the platform team has a specific diagnostic starting point instead of starting the investigation over from nothing

questions.questionText: What does Practice Loop step 3 — counting how many checklist items have a real attached artifact versus how many are self-certified — actually accomplish?

options.optionText: It calculates the total cost of running the go-live sign-off meeting

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, why would onboarding a fourth tenant still likely need the original FDE's involvement for at least one checklist category, even though Meridian's own platform team now owns ongoing operations?
questions.explanation: The extension distinguishes repeatable operational verification (which the platform team can run unchanged) from genuinely customer-specific negotiation (which still needs the judgment the FDE role was built around).

questions.questionText: Why is BYOK via a cross-account KMS grant the correct response to the healthcare customer's brief, rather than a full single-tenant deployment?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the deployment-topologies lesson's Globex example directly — matching the response to the specifically named requirement, not defaulting toward maximal isolation.

options.optionText: Single-tenant deployments are technically incompatible with healthcare data under any circumstances

The brief's named requirement is key control specifically, not physical infrastructure isolation — BYOK satisfies the actual stated constraint without the added operational cost of a dedicated stack the brief never asked for
BYOK is always the cheaper option regardless of what the brief actually specifies
A single-tenant deployment does not support encryption at all

questions.questionText: In part two of the assessment, what specific evidence should lead you to diagnose connection-pool exhaustion rather than a raw compute limit as the bottleneck?
questions.explanation: The assessment applies the same diagnostic signature (timeouts with low CPU) taught in the load-testing lesson, now to an unfamiliar scenario rather than the familiar Meridian narrative.

options.optionText: The incident narrative directly states "connection pool" as the cause, with no other evidence needed

Failures cluster as timeouts at a fixed concurrency threshold while CPU stays well under capacity — the specific failure-mode signature that points at the pool, not compute, consistent with the load-testing lesson's diagnostic method
The application's error logs report a generic "internal server error" with no further detail
The k6 test's total request count was lower than expected

questions.questionText: What is the assessment asking you to demonstrate by requiring both an internal blameless postmortem and a customer-facing RCA for the same incident?
questions.explanation: This directly tests the incident-response lesson's core distinction — the assessment wants to see the learner apply that differentiation, not just produce two similar documents.

options.optionText: That the two documents should be identical, just formatted differently

That you can correctly differentiate what each document should and shouldn't carry — the postmortem's full technical candor and process-gap focus versus the RCA's plain-language, non-attributing, customer-appropriate content
That only the RCA needs to be accurate; the postmortem can be approximate
That the postmortem should be written first and then simply translated word-for-word into the RCA

questions.questionText: What sequencing gap does the assessment's part-two incident narrative reproduce, per the scenario?
questions.explanation: This is the same sequencing-gap pattern from the incident-response lesson's Globex scenario, applied here to an unfamiliar customer to test whether the learner recognizes the pattern rather than just recalling the original example.

options.optionText: The fix for the connection-pool issue was never actually identified before the incident occurred
The fix was tested but not yet deployed when a real customer traffic spike hit the same threshold the load test had already found, three days before the fix was scheduled to ship
The incident had no relationship to any previously identified risk

questions.questionText: Why does the assessment require you to name at least three specific gaps between your work and genuine production readiness, rather than treating a complete, well-written assessment as evidence the design is production-ready?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the same self-evaluation discipline established elsewhere in the FDE curriculum's assessment lessons — honest, specific gap identification is itself the skill being tested.

options.optionText: Every assessment submission is expected to be fully production-ready regardless of its scaled-down scope

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what should the go-live checklist item you write for your single most important self-evaluation gap actually include?
questions.explanation: The extension asks the learner to apply the previous lesson's checklist discipline directly — a checklist item is only meaningful with a real, attached verification artifact, not a vague future intent.

A real, attached verification artifact requirement, per the go-live lesson's evidence-over-assertion discipline — not a self-certified assertion that the gap has been closed
A reference to the original Meridian ClauseReview engagement, since this assessment's mock customer is the same as ClauseReview's

questions.questionText: What does PACELC's "Else" (E) branch force a system designer to reason about that CAP theorem alone is silent on?
questions.explanation: CAP is entirely about partition behavior; PACELC's "Else" branch is specifically the non-partition case, where a system still pays a latency-vs-consistency cost on every request.

options.optionText: What happens when a system has zero nodes remaining after a failure
The latency-versus-consistency trade-off a system pays in the common case, when no partition is happening at all
Whether a system should use SQL or NoSQL for its primary datastore
How many replicas a system needs to survive a single disk failure

questions.questionText: Per the lesson's multi-region SaaS framing, what is the real cost being traded off between a single-writer-region design and a multi-writer active-active design?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's concrete PACELC application — the cost isn't abstract, it's a specific choice between paying latency on every distant write versus taking on real conflict-resolution complexity.

options.optionText: Single-writer designs are always cheaper to host regardless of traffic patterns

Single-writer pays cross-region write latency on every distant write but stays simple to reason about; active-active gives every region local write latency but requires an explicit conflict-resolution strategy for concurrent writes to the same record
Active-active designs never need a conflict-resolution strategy because Postgres handles it automatically
Single-writer designs cannot serve read traffic from any region other than the primary

questions.questionText: What specific failure does Raft's monotonically increasing term number prevent?
questions.explanation: Term numbers are Raft's concrete mechanism against split-brain: any node seeing a higher term recognizes its own leadership claim as stale and steps down, which is what CAP's abstract "choose C" framing doesn't actually implement on its own.

options.optionText: A follower node running out of disk space during log replication
Split-brain — two nodes both believing they are the current leader and both accepting writes, typically after a partition heals; a node encountering a higher term steps down immediately
A client sending a malformed write request to the cluster
The cluster losing all its data if the network is ever partitioned

questions.questionText: What is the core trade-off between an orchestration-based saga and a choreography-based saga, per the lesson?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's exact trade-off statement — centralized visibility and complexity versus no single point of logic but a scattered failure path.

options.optionText: Orchestration-based sagas cannot use compensating actions, only choreography-based ones can

Orchestration centralizes workflow logic and visibility in one coordinator at the cost of that component owning real complexity; choreography has no single point of workflow logic but scatters the failure path across services with no one place to read it
Choreography-based sagas are always faster because they have no coordinator to call
Orchestration-based sagas require a distributed two-phase commit across all systems involved

questions.questionText: In the `ContractApprovalSaga` scenario, why does the CLM-creation step's retry, carrying an `(org_id, event_id)` idempotency key, not create a second CLM record even though the original request actually succeeded before the orchestrator's timeout?
questions.explanation: This is the specific mechanism: an idempotency key lets a retried call be recognized as a duplicate of an already-applied effect, which is exactly why a compensation or a forward step is safe to replay with one.

options.optionText: CLM systems automatically reject any request made more than once, regardless of its contents
The idempotency key lets the retried request be recognized as a duplicate of a request that already completed, so the same effect is not applied twice
The orchestrator waits indefinitely for the first request instead of ever retrying
Compensating actions are only ever needed for the first step of a saga, never a retry of it

questions.questionText: Why does the `ContractApprovalSaga`'s compensation for a failed e-signature step mark the already-created CLM record `cancelled` rather than delete it?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific point is about what a compensation should semantically communicate — a visible, correctly-labeled void state, not an erasure that could confuse anyone who already saw the record.

options.optionText: Deleting records is technically impossible in most CLM systems
A human may have already seen the record; clearly labeling it void is a more accurate and auditable compensation than making it disappear as though it never existed
Marking a record cancelled is always faster to execute than deleting it
CLM systems require every record to remain in the system permanently by law

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what specifically becomes harder once the `ContractApprovalSaga` is redesigned as choreography instead of orchestration?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's named cost of choreography: centralized state visibility, which an orchestrator gives essentially for free, has to be reconstructed some other way (e.g., a read-side projection) once no component is coordinating in one place.

options.optionText: Each individual system's own local transaction becomes impossible to complete

Answering "what is the current state of approval X across all three systems, right now" — trivial to read from an orchestrator's own state, and genuinely harder to reconstruct once no single component tracks the whole workflow
Compensating actions can no longer be defined for any step in the workflow
Idempotency keys stop working once there is no central coordinator

questions.questionText: What does the lesson mean by a capacity estimate needing to be "load-bearing" rather than merely precise?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is about the estimate's role in justifying design choices, not about numerical precision — a rough but load-bearing number beats a precise one nobody's decision actually depends on.

options.optionText: The estimate must be calculated to the exact byte and query, with no rounding permitted
Every later design decision should be able to point back to a specific number in the estimate and explain why that number, not a different one, drove the choice
The estimate should only ever be produced by a senior engineer, never a junior one
The estimate must be verified against production traffic before any design work can begin

questions.questionText: Per the lesson, what becomes a genuinely new design question at this scale that a single-tenant or small-scale RAG deployment never has to answer?
questions.explanation: Pre-filtering (not post-filtering) is always correct regardless of scale — Phase 12 already established this. What's new at this scale is a physical partitioning decision: where a tenant's vectors actually live in the index topology.

options.optionText: Where in the physical index a tenant's vectors actually live, and how that partitioning scheme affects noisy-neighbor risk and staleness handling
Whether retrieval should be pre-filtered or post-filtered by tenant, since post-filtering is only unsafe at large scale
Whether hybrid search should combine dense and sparse retrieval, since that only matters above a certain document count
Whether RAGAS scoring is necessary, since evaluation is only needed once a system serves multiple tenants

questions.questionText: Per the lesson's capacity estimate, why does the 2-second p99 latency budget leave enough headroom to afford both a reranking pass and a semantic-cache check?
questions.explanation: The lesson's itemized stage-by-stage budget is what makes the "affordable" claim concrete rather than asserted — summing the stages shows genuine headroom under 2 seconds.

options.optionText: Reranking and caching cost no additional latency under any circumstances
The itemized budget (embedding ~50-100ms, retrieval ~50-150ms, reranking ~100-150ms, generation ~500-1000ms streamed) sums to well under 2 seconds, leaving real room for these additions
The 2-second budget only applies to the embedding and retrieval stages, not to generation
Semantic caching eliminates the need for a latency budget entirely

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson recommend routing only some queries through the reranking pass, rather than running it unconditionally on every query?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific argument is about wasted latency on queries that don't benefit — a complexity-based routing check decides per-query whether reranking is worth its cost, mirroring the model-tier routing discipline from Phase 12.

options.optionText: Reranking is deprecated and should never be used in a production RAG system

A simple factoid query that hybrid retrieval already answers correctly gains no accuracy from reranking, so running it unconditionally wastes 100-150ms of the latency budget for no benefit on that class of query
Reranking cannot run on queries shorter than a certain length
Running reranking on every query would exceed the storage budget, not the latency budget

questions.questionText: What should happen to a query's retrieval path when the embedding service is unavailable, per the lesson's failure-mode design?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific design is graceful degradation, not failure — hybrid search's dual (dense + sparse) design is exactly what makes a keyword-only fallback available.

options.optionText: The entire request should fail immediately with an error, since retrieval cannot function without embeddings

The query should degrade to keyword-only (BM25) search rather than fail outright, since a worse answer beats no answer and this is exactly what hybrid search's keyword component was designed to survive
The request should be silently dropped with no response returned to the caller
The system should wait indefinitely for the embedding service to recover before responding

questions.questionText: Why does a single tenant's bulk upload of 50,000 documents overnight not delay another tenant's ingestion, per the lesson's design?
questions.explanation: Per-tenant partitioning and rate limits in the ingestion pipeline are the specific mechanism the lesson names to prevent this from becoming a platform-wide incident.

options.optionText: Bulk uploads are processed at a lower priority than all other traffic system-wide, regardless of tenant
The ingestion pipeline is partitioned per tenant with per-tenant rate limits, preventing one tenant's volume from consuming capacity that another tenant's ingestion needs
Only one tenant is permitted to upload documents at any given time across the entire platform
Document ingestion has no capacity limits at all in this design

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what kind of metric should trigger migrating a tenant from the shared long-tail index to a dedicated shard?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the lesson's broader insistence on evidence-driven decisions — the migration trigger should be a measured signal, not an arbitrary schedule or a reactive response to a complaint.

options.optionText: The tenant's billing tier alone, regardless of any measured technical impact

A metric tied to actual scale or impact — document count, query volume, or measured latency impact on shard-mates — so the migration happens based on evidence rather than being noticed only after it becomes a problem
A fixed calendar schedule migrating one tenant per quarter regardless of size
Whichever tenant complains first, regardless of whether their usage has actually grown

questions.questionText: What additional governance dimension does a 50-tenant agentic platform need beyond the per-client resource/tool scoping Phase 13's MCP lesson already designed for a single customer?
questions.explanation: The lesson draws a direct parallel to Phase 15's RLS argument — tenant scoping at the tool-integration layer needs the same structural rigor as tenant scoping at the database layer, not a shared ACL that happens to include everyone.

options.optionText: MCP servers must be rewritten to support a completely different protocol at platform scale

Which tenant's traffic is allowed to reach which tenant's own MCP server instance at all — a single shared server per system type with one shared access-control list would risk exactly the cross-tenant leak Phase 15's RLS lesson closed at the database layer
Whether resources, tools, and prompts should be merged into a single MCP primitive at scale
Whether MCP servers need to support synchronous calls, since they only supported asynchronous ones for a single customer

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson choose a shared worker pool with per-tenant fair-share scheduling over a fully dedicated pool per tenant, for the 50-tenant platform?
questions.explanation: The lesson's explicit trade-off is compute efficiency (shared pool) against operational overhead (50 dedicated pools) — fair-share scheduling is what lets the platform get the efficiency without the noisy-neighbor risk.

options.optionText: Dedicated pools are technically impossible to implement for an agentic workflow platform

A shared pool is dramatically more compute-efficient given the uneven, mostly-waiting workload profile, and per-tenant concurrency caps bound the noisy-neighbor risk without the operational overhead of 50 fully separate pools
Fair-share scheduling eliminates the need for per-tenant MCP server scoping entirely
Dedicated pools would violate the platform's human-in-the-loop requirements

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson design workflow-state coordination (which orchestrator instance owns a given workflow's next step) as CP rather than AP?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's explicit contrast with Lesson 2's RAG index — the correct consistency model is a property of what a specific failure would cost (double-executing a tool call here versus stale search results there), not a platform-wide default.

options.optionText: CP is always the correct default for any data path in a distributed system

Two orchestrator instances both believing they own the same workflow's next step would double-execute a tool call — an outcome the system cannot tolerate, unlike the vector index's staleness in Lesson 2, which was an acceptable AP trade
Workflow state changes so rarely that consistency has no real cost either way
AP designs are incompatible with human-in-the-loop approval gates

questions.questionText: What should the model-routing gateway do when the primary LLM provider becomes unavailable, per the lesson's failure-mode design?
questions.explanation: The lesson's design is a circuit breaker with failover, consistent with the model-routing gateway's reliability discipline from Phase 12, not a stall or a silent drop.

options.optionText: Stall every in-flight workflow waiting on that provider until it recovers, with no fallback

Immediately terminate every in-flight workflow across all 50 tenants
Silently drop the failing requests with no retry or fallback of any kind

questions.questionText: Why does a workflow retrying a failing tool call need a bounded retry count and a dead-letter state, rather than retrying indefinitely?
questions.explanation: The lesson connects this directly to the fair-share scheduling design — an unbounded retry loop is exactly the noisy-neighbor failure mode the per-tenant concurrency cap is meant to prevent, and a dead-letter state is what makes the problem visible instead of silently ongoing.

options.optionText: Bounded retries are required by every LLM provider's terms of service
An indefinitely retrying workflow consumes its tenant's fair-share concurrency budget forever, degrading that tenant's own other workflows without ever surfacing the problem to a human
Tool calls can only be retried a maximum of three times by protocol design
Dead-letter states are only relevant for workflows involving a human-in-the-loop gate

questions.questionText: Why must a tool call that times out from the orchestrator's perspective but actually succeeded downstream be protected by an idempotency key?
questions.explanation: This is the same idempotency discipline from Phase 13's tool-contract lesson, applied here to the specific timeout-vs-actual-success ambiguity a retry has no other way to resolve safely.

options.optionText: Idempotency keys are required by MCP's protocol specification for every call

Without one, a retry of the timed-out call would execute the side-effecting action (a refund, a deal-stage update) a second time, since the orchestrator has no way to know the first attempt already succeeded
Idempotency keys make tool calls execute faster on retry
This scenario cannot actually occur once workflow state is stored in a CP data path

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, when one tenant requires physically isolated compute for compliance reasons, which piece of the platform's design actually has to change?
questions.explanation: Because MCP scoping and workflow-state ownership were already designed per-tenant, only the physical compute-routing layer needs to change for this one tenant — the lesson's point is that good tenant-isolation design at the right layers means a compliance requirement like this is a narrow, contained change, not a platform-wide rearchitecture.

options.optionText: The workflow-state consistency model must switch from CP to AP for every tenant, not just this one

questions.questionText: Per the lesson, what is the actual constraint that breaks a naive database-per-tenant design well before a few hundred tenants?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is about connection pooling, not compute or query performance — a pooling proxy that multiplexes logical tenant connections is what actually makes DB-per-tenant viable at real scale.

options.optionText: Postgres cannot technically run more than 100 separate databases on one cluster

Connection pool exhaustion — a one-reserved-pool-per-database model runs into a hard connection ceiling long before compute becomes the bottleneck, requiring a connection-pooling proxy that multiplexes tenant connections
Query performance inherently degrades once more than 100 databases exist on a single server
Database-per-tenant designs cannot support point-in-time restore at any scale

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson use the 4,900/90/10 tenant-size breakdown to justify the three-tier isolation design, rather than choosing a tier count arbitrarily?
questions.explanation: The capacity estimate is the load-bearing evidence for the tiering decision — the lesson explicitly ties the tier boundaries to the measured skew in tenant size, not to an arbitrary or universal tier count.

options.optionText: Three tiers is simply the industry-standard number regardless of any specific platform's tenant distribution

The breakdown shows the actual skew — a handful of enterprise tenants hold data volume and SLA requirements dramatically different from the long tail, which is the concrete evidence that treating all tenants uniformly would either over-provision for the small tenants or under-serve the large ones
