questions.questionText: What specific noisy-neighbor scenario does a per-tenant-role `statement_timeout` in the shared-RLS tier prevent?
questions.explanation: This is the specific mechanism-to-failure mapping the lesson requires — a statement timeout bounds how long one runaway query can hold shared resources, distinct from RLS (which is about row-level access, not resource consumption).

options.optionText: A tenant exceeding their contracted total storage quota
One tenant's accidentally unindexed, full-table-scanning query holding a connection and CPU indefinitely, degrading every other tenant sharing the same infrastructure
A tenant attempting to read another tenant's rows without an RLS policy in place
Two tenants signing up with the same email domain

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist a tenant's move from shared-RLS to schema-per-tenant should be driven by an evidenced trigger metric, rather than decided once at signup?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific argument is evidence-over-guesswork — a signup-time guess is unreliable, while a measured signal (volume, load, contract) is something the platform can actually act on correctly and at the right time.

options.optionText: Because Postgres technically prevents migrating a tenant between isolation tiers after signup

Because a sales conversation's guess about eventual tenant size at signup is unreliable, while data volume, sustained load against the shared tier's guardrails, or an actual contractual requirement are measurable signals the platform can act on when they actually occur
Because every tenant eventually needs to migrate to the most isolated tier regardless of actual size
Because tier migration is only possible once a tenant reaches the enterprise size class

questions.questionText: Why does a single enterprise-scale tenant landing in the shared-RLS tier by an onboarding mistake risk a platform-wide outage?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is capacity mismatch — the shared tier's guardrails are calibrated for the long tail, and an enterprise-scale tenant's usage can exceed what those guardrails were sized to absorb, directly threatening every tenant sharing that infrastructure.

options.optionText: Enterprise tenants are technically incompatible with the RLS mechanism and cause immediate query errors

The shared tier's guardrails (statement timeouts, connection caps, read-replica routing) are sized for the long tail's typical usage, and a whale-scale tenant's usage spike can exceed them in ways that degrade every other tenant sharing that infrastructure
Whale tenants always have more support tickets than small tenants, overwhelming the support team
A whale tenant in the shared tier automatically triggers a schema migration for every other tenant

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say schema-per-tenant makes a point-in-time restore of one specific tenant's data tractable in a way shared-schema RLS fundamentally doesn't?
questions.explanation: The mechanism is structural: a schema boundary aligns exactly with a tenant boundary, so a restore operation scoped to a schema naturally scopes to one tenant — something a shared-table restore cannot do without restoring every tenant's rows in that table.

options.optionText: Schema-per-tenant databases are backed up more frequently than shared-schema databases by default

Each tenant's data lives in its own schema, so restoring that schema restores exactly and only that tenant's data; a shared-schema restore would restore every tenant's data at once, since they all live in the same tables
RLS makes point-in-time restore technically impossible for any tenant under any circumstances
Schema-per-tenant tenants are not permitted to request a restore at all

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, what specific risk does building a combined cross-tenant reporting view (for an acquiring company's two tenants) reintroduce that the rest of this lesson's design was built to avoid?
questions.explanation: This is the tension the extension is designed to surface — a legitimate cross-tenant feature has to be built as a narrow, explicit exception, not by loosening the isolation guarantees this entire lesson was built to establish.

options.optionText: The risk that connection pooling becomes unnecessary once cross-tenant queries are allowed

The exact cross-tenant data-leak risk RLS and schema isolation were built to prevent — a feature that deliberately reads across tenant boundaries needs its own carefully scoped, explicit exception rather than weakening the underlying isolation guarantee for either tenant more broadly
The risk that the acquiring company's dedicated database will run out of storage
The risk that schema-per-tenant migrations will fail for unrelated tenants

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson choose at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers over building exactly-once delivery into the hub's event bus?
questions.explanation: The lesson's argument is pragmatic, not theoretical impossibility — at-least-once plus idempotency achieves the needed safety without the operational cost of building genuine exactly-once semantics.

options.optionText: Exactly-once delivery is theoretically impossible in any distributed messaging system

Exactly-once delivery is real infrastructure to build and operate correctly at 20+-system scale, while at-least-once paired with idempotency keys (already required for connector writes) achieves the same practical safety with far less operational complexity
At-least-once delivery is always faster than exactly-once delivery under any load
Idempotent consumers are only needed for batch connectors, not event-driven ones

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist each of the 20+ connectors be decided individually as webhook-driven or batch, rather than forcing all connectors onto one uniform topology?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is a per-system freshness-requirement decision (Phase 13's axis), not a preference for one pattern — a uniform default would force a wrong trade-off onto systems whose actual requirement doesn't match it.

options.optionText: Because the event bus technically cannot support more than one delivery pattern at a time

Because each system's actual downstream freshness requirement differs — forcing a uniform topology would impose a wrong trade-off on whichever category of system doesn't fit it (e.g., forcing batch on a support system needing near-real-time state)
Because webhook-driven connectors are always superior and batch should only be used when webhooks are technically unavailable
Because HR and finance systems are incapable of supporting webhook delivery under any circumstances

questions.questionText: Why does running entity resolution as one standing hub service, rather than per point-to-point pair, matter more at 20+ systems than it would for just two or three?
questions.explanation: This directly extends the hub's core "build once" argument from raw connectivity to identity resolution specifically — the payoff scales with the number of systems that would otherwise each need their own resolution logic.

options.optionText: Entity resolution is only technically possible once a hub-based topology is in place

A point-to-point design would require reimplementing resolution logic redundantly at up to 190 pairs; centralizing it means it is built once and correctly serves every consumer, the same "build once, serve all" argument the hub makes for connectivity itself
Entity resolution becomes unnecessary once more than 10 systems share the same hub
Centralized entity resolution eliminates the need for any human review of ambiguous matches

questions.questionText: What specifically prevents one connector's outage from halting the bus for every other one of the 20+ systems?
questions.explanation: This is the specific failure-isolation mechanism the lesson names — per-connector circuit breaking and dead-lettering, not a shared fate across all connectors.

options.optionText: The event bus automatically restarts every connector simultaneously whenever one fails
Each connector runs behind its own circuit breaker with its own dead-letter queue, so a failed connector's errors are isolated to that connector rather than blocking the bus's shared infrastructure
Only one connector is permitted to be active on the bus at any given time
Connectors do not communicate with the bus directly, so their failures cannot affect it

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson design a slow downstream consumer (e.g., the entity-resolution service falling behind) to apply backpressure rather than buffer unboundedly?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific concern is bounding the failure — an unbounded backlog is a slow-motion hub-wide incident, while bounded backpressure with alerting surfaces the problem while it's still contained.

options.optionText: Backpressure makes the slow consumer process events faster automatically

Unbounded buffering would let the backlog silently grow until the hub itself runs out of memory or disk, while a bounded queue with lag alerting surfaces the problem before it becomes a hub-wide incident
Backpressure is only relevant for batch connectors, never for event-driven ones
Buffering is technically unsupported by any event bus implementation

questions.questionText: In the Practice Loop's deal-closing saga, if the ERP invoice step succeeds but the ITSM onboarding-ticket step then fails, what should the saga do?
questions.explanation: This is Lesson 1's saga-compensation discipline applied directly — a failed later step triggers the compensating action for the already-succeeded earlier step, never a silent, unreconciled state mismatch.

options.optionText: Leave the ERP invoice in place with no record of the ITSM failure, since the invoice itself succeeded

Run the ERP step's compensating action (reverse or flag the invoice for reconciliation) per the saga pattern, rather than leave the two systems' states silently disagreeing with no record of the discrepancy
Immediately retry the entire saga from the beginning an unlimited number of times until it succeeds
Delete the CRM deal record entirely so the workflow never appears to have started

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, when a newly-acquired subsidiary's CRM joins the hub with no shared ID structure against the existing 20 systems, what specifically has to change?
questions.explanation: Because the hub's core components (bus, connector abstraction, saga orchestrator) are already system-agnostic by design, onboarding a new system is a contained change — the real new work is specific to entity resolution, which needs new matching signals for records with no shared ID structure.

options.optionText: The event bus's core architecture must be rebuilt to support a 21st system, since it was hard-coded for exactly 20

The entity-resolution service needs new corroborating signals to match the subsidiary's records against the existing crosswalk (since exact-key matching won't work); the bus, connector abstraction layer, and saga orchestrator need no structural change to onboard the new connector
Every existing connector must be rewritten to support the subsidiary's authentication protocol
The saga orchestrator must switch from orchestration to choreography once a 21st system is added

questions.questionText: Why does the framework insist on requirements clarification before any diagram is drawn, rather than starting with a high-level design and adjusting it as requirements surface?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is about the cost of a wrong assumption discovered mid-diagram — clarifying first is cheaper than redesigning live once the interviewer reveals a requirement the candidate assumed incorrectly.

options.optionText: Interviewers penalize any candidate who does not ask at least three questions, regardless of relevance
A design built against an assumed requirement is one wrong assumption away from a live redesign under time pressure, while clarifying first avoids that cost entirely
Diagrams are not permitted until the interviewer explicitly requests one
Capacity estimation cannot be performed correctly unless a diagram already exists

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, what distinguishes a capacity estimate that demonstrates seniority from one that reads as a memorized ritual?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly frames the estimate's value as its downstream effect on a real decision (partitioning, caching) — a number computed and discarded signals rote practice, not judgment.

options.optionText: Using more decimal places of precision in the final calculated number
The estimate is used to change a specific subsequent design decision, rather than being computed and then never referenced again
Performing the estimate as quickly as possible to save interview time
Citing an industry-standard benchmark number instead of deriving one from the prompt's stated inputs

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson argue that most candidates over-invest time in the high-level design (box-diagram) stage relative to its actual interview weight?
questions.explanation: The lesson's claim is about where interview signal actually concentrates — the deep-dive reveals whether a candidate can reason about a specific hard problem, which the box diagram alone cannot show.

options.optionText: Interviewers do not read the diagram at all and only evaluate verbal answers
The diagram exists mainly to establish shared vocabulary for the deep-dive that follows, and the deep-dive — not the diagram — is where the interview is actually won or lost
A diagram with more than four boxes is considered a failing answer
High-level design is only relevant for distributed-systems-specific prompts, not general ones

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say a candidate who presents only one approach to a deep-dive component, framed as the only reasonable one, signals inexperience — even if that approach happens to be correct?
questions.explanation: The lesson's reasoning is about what the omission reveals, not about the correctness of the single answer given — being right by luck or memorization is indistinguishable from being right by judgment unless alternatives are shown and weighed.

options.optionText: Interviewers always prefer the second approach a candidate mentions over the first
Production systems almost never have exactly one viable design, and an engineer who cannot see the alternatives cannot be trusted to have picked correctly among them
A single approach takes less time to explain, which interviewers penalize
Presenting one approach violates a formal rule of the interview format

questions.questionText: What does counting how many deep-dive follow-up questions a high-level design would survive without a redesign actually reveal, per the Practice Loop's diagnostic step?
questions.explanation: This diagnostic step is a visceral, measurable check on design robustness — it distinguishes a diagram that only looks complete from one that would actually survive the interviewer's real scrutiny.

options.optionText: How aesthetically clean the diagram looks compared to a typical candidate's
Which parts of the design are load-bearing and which are decoration that would not hold up once the interviewer steers into a specific hard problem
The exact number of boxes the diagram should contain
Whether the candidate should have asked more clarifying questions at the very start

questions.questionText: The Suggested Extension asks you to predict a likely deep-dive question for one of the module's earlier System Design scenario lessons (RAG at Scale, Agentic Platform at Scale, Multi-Tenant SaaS, Enterprise Integration Hub). What should that prediction be based on, according to the lesson's own framework?
questions.explanation: A deep-dive question targets the genuinely hard trade-off in a design, not an arbitrary component — predicting it means identifying which part of the prior lesson's design actually carried that difficulty.

options.optionText: Whichever component happens to appear first in that lesson's high-level design diagram
What that lesson's worked example already identified as the hardest, most consequential part of the design — the same signal an interviewer's steering question is meant to surface
A randomly chosen component, since deep-dive questions cannot be predicted in advance
The component requiring the fewest lines of code to implement

questions.questionText: Derek Nomura opens the discovery call with "we want AI to speed up underwriting." Why does the FDE run the current-state walkthrough instead of scoping directly against that sentence?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the discovery-call lesson's core claim: a stakeholder's solution-shaped framing can differ from the process-level pain only the people living the process daily can accurately report.

options.optionText: Derek's request was considered dishonest and needed independent verification
A solution-shaped request from a champion can obscure the more specific underlying pain, which only surfaces by asking the people who actually perform the process daily
AI-based solutions are never appropriate for underwriting workflows
Current-state walkthroughs are a mandatory legal step for any AI engagement

questions.questionText: What requirement did the underwriters themselves surface that neither Sandra's nor Derek's framing captured?
questions.explanation: This is the stakeholder-mapping payoff made concrete: the end users' real concern (verifiable evidence before staking professional judgment) differs from both the economic buyer's and the champion's framing, and only surfaces because they were asked directly.

options.optionText: A demand for a higher salary tied to the new system's rollout
The need to be able to check the underlying evidence behind a recommendation before staking their own name on a bind decision, distinct from turnaround time or adoption metrics
A request that the system be built entirely in-house rather than by an external FDE
A preference for a slower rollout timeline than Sandra proposed

questions.questionText: The lesson explicitly distinguishes general counsel's no-auto-bind requirement from a phase-one simplification that might be relaxed later. Why does this distinction matter for scoping?
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that this constraint is permanent and non-negotiable, which is exactly why it drives the architecture choice (the hybrid) rather than being treated as a target to relax once the model looks accurate in a demo.

options.optionText: Phase-one simplifications are always compliance-driven by definition
It is a hard, non-negotiable compliance constraint that must shape the chosen architecture itself, not a convenience choice that could be revisited once the system proves accurate
The constraint only applies until Coastal Underwriters onboards as a second tenant
General counsel's constraints are advisory and can be overridden by Sandra as the economic buyer

questions.questionText: What makes the risk register's first entry ("the grounded-extraction pipeline hallucinates a schedule-of-values total") a well-formed risk entry per this lesson's standard?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the risk-register discipline from Module 5: a falsifiable, concrete entry with likelihood, impact, mitigation, and owner is what makes a risk actually trackable and closeable.

options.optionText: It states a vague possibility of "data quality issues" without further detail
It names a concrete, falsifiable failure mode with a likelihood, impact, specific mitigation (evidence quote and source page checked before reaching a reviewer), and a named owner
It assigns blame to Meridian's underwriting team rather than the FDE
It avoids naming any mitigation, leaving that decision for Sprint 2

questions.questionText: Why does the FDE send the discovery brief and PRD-lite back to Sandra, Derek, and the underwriting team before Sprint 2's build work begins?
questions.explanation: This directly extends the discovery-brief-confirmation discipline from Module 5: the earliest possible point to catch a scope misunderstanding is also the cheapest.

options.optionText: It is a purely ceremonial step with no bearing on the engagement's outcome

Confirming the documents before building is the cheapest point to catch a misunderstanding — a dispute caught here costs a re-read, while the same dispute caught after a working prototype costs rebuilt work
It transfers full legal liability for the project's outcome to Meridian
It is required only because Coastal Underwriters is involved in the engagement

questions.questionText: The PRD-lite's non-goals section explicitly excludes personal-lines support and direct Atlas write access. What specific dispute does stating these exclusions explicitly prevent, compared to leaving them unstated?
questions.explanation: This is the same non-goals discipline from Module 5's scoping lesson: leaving something unmentioned does not communicate exclusion, it leaves the reader free to assume it was included.

options.optionText: A dispute about which programming language the extraction pipeline is built in
A stakeholder later assuming one of those capabilities was included in phase one because it was never explicitly excluded, discovered only once the system is demoed
A dispute about Coastal Underwriters' contractual payment terms
A disagreement over who owns the final source code repository

questions.questionText: Why does the review-queue frontend need zero changes when the real extraction pipeline replaces the hardcoded stub?
questions.explanation: This is the specific payoff of a well-designed stub: matching output shape lets frontend work proceed in parallel and survive the later swap without rework.

options.optionText: The review queue does not actually read any data produced by either the stub or the real pipeline

The stub and the real pipeline are deliberately built to emit data in the identical shape, so the frontend that was built and tested against the stub already handles the real pipeline's output correctly
The stub and the real pipeline share the exact same underlying LLM extraction code
Frontend changes are always deferred until after the real pipeline exists, regardless of shape

questions.questionText: What happens to an extracted field whose `evidence_quote` doesn't literally match the corresponding OCR'd source page text?
questions.explanation: The grounding check's whole purpose is preventing an ungrounded value from silently entering the pipeline at a confidence it hasn't earned — it routes to human review instead of being auto-approved or discarded.

options.optionText: It is automatically corrected by the LLM on a second extraction attempt
It is rejected by the grounding check and routed to a human-review lane rather than reaching the recommendation step at a falsely high confidence
It is silently dropped from the extraction output with no further action
It is flagged but still allowed to proceed directly into the recommend-worker's tool calls

questions.questionText: Why does the `recommend-worker`'s output sit behind a blocking human-in-the-loop gate rather than a human-on-the-loop monitoring posture, unlike the `intake-summary-worker`?
questions.explanation: This directly applies the multi-agent curriculum's hard-to-reverse-consequence criterion: a reversible, low-stakes worker proceeds unblocked while a worker whose output carries real consequence needs the blocking gate.

options.optionText: The recommend-worker is technically slower to run than the intake-summary-worker
A wrong bind recommendation has a real-money, hard-to-reverse consequence, which is exactly the criterion that determines which worker in an orchestrator-worker system needs a blocking gate
General counsel requires every worker in the system to have a blocking gate, without exception
The intake-summary-worker does not use any LLM calls, unlike the recommend-worker

questions.questionText: How does Sprint 2's design turn general counsel's no-auto-bind constraint from Sprint 1 into a structural property of SubmissionIQ, rather than a policy someone has to remember to enforce?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is architectural: a constraint enforced by the absence of an executing code path is more durable than one enforced only by policy or a reminder, which someone could eventually bypass or forget.

options.optionText: By adding a comment in the code reminding future engineers not to remove the approval step
By making the recommend-worker's output a proposal only, with no code path that lets it execute a bind action without first passing through the blocking human-approval gate
By requiring general counsel to personally review every single submission before it reaches an underwriter
By logging every recommendation for a quarterly compliance audit after the fact

questions.questionText: Why does `AtlasConnector` use cursor-based pagination for exposure lookups instead of offset-based pagination?
questions.explanation: This reuses the connector-design curriculum's exact reasoning: cursor pagination stays correct as records change mid-fetch, while offset pagination silently skips or duplicates records under the same conditions.

options.optionText: Cursor pagination is always faster than offset pagination regardless of data volatility
Meridian's exposure data changes continuously during business hours, and offset pagination's correctness assumption — a static, unchanging list — does not hold in that environment
Atlas's API does not technically support offset-based query parameters
Cursor pagination is required by the JWT bearer OAuth flow AtlasConnector uses

questions.questionText: During the Atlas maintenance window, why does the `recommend-worker` surface findings with a note about unavailable exposure data instead of hanging the submission review indefinitely?
questions.explanation: This is the timeout/circuit-breaker discipline from the agentic-systems curriculum applied to a real downstream outage: fail fast into a deterministic, visible fallback rather than hanging indefinitely.

options.optionText: Atlas maintenance windows are announced far enough in advance that the system pre-emptively pauses all reviews

The tool-calling loop applies the same timeout-and-circuit-breaker pattern established for agentic tool calls, so a degraded downstream dependency fails fast into a deterministic fallback instead of stalling the whole run
The underwriter review queue automatically retries the entire submission from scratch every five minutes
Exposure data is not actually required for any recommendation, so its unavailability has no effect

questions.questionText: Why does `atlas-mcp-server` wrap `AtlasConnector` once instead of letting every individual tool handler that needs Atlas data reimplement OAuth refresh and pagination itself?
questions.explanation: This is the layered-separation argument from the curriculum applied one level deeper: an MCP server's tool handler calls into a connector rather than reimplementing OAuth and pagination itself, keeping that plumbing in exactly one place.

options.optionText: MCP servers are technically incapable of calling a shared connector abstraction

Keeping system-specific plumbing in one place, rather than scattered across every tool handler that touches Atlas, is the same separation-of-concerns argument the MCP and connector-design curriculum both made for keeping integration mechanics out of business logic
Reimplementing OAuth refresh in every tool handler is required for compliance with general counsel's constraint
Connector abstractions are only useful when more than three tools need the same system

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist on connecting explicitly as Coastal's tenant context and asserting Meridian's rows are absent, rather than only checking that Coastal's own data is present and correct?
questions.explanation: This reuses the multi-tenant curriculum's exact testing discipline: RLS is a security boundary, and a boundary test that never checks the negative case can pass while silently leaking.

options.optionText: Postgres does not support querying as a specific tenant context at all
A test that only checks the correct tenant's own data is present can pass even while a leak of another tenant's data alongside it goes completely unnoticed, since nobody asserted the negative case
Positive-case tests are always slower to run than negative-case tests
FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY cannot be verified without a negative-case query

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say per-tenant Celery queue routing was applied only once Coastal Underwriters was a real, onboarded tenant, rather than being built during Sprint 2 against Meridian alone?
questions.explanation: This reuses the build-sequencing argument from the enterprise-document-review-app lesson: a mitigation for a problem that doesn't yet exist has nothing real to validate it against.

options.optionText: Celery does not technically support per-tenant queue routing until a certain traffic volume is reached

Building queue routing against a single tenant would have nothing real to validate it against — the noisy-neighbor problem it solves only exists once a second tenant's traffic can actually contend for shared capacity
Per-tenant routing was legally required to wait until Coastal's contract was fully signed
Meridian explicitly requested that queue routing be delayed until Coastal's onboarding

questions.questionText: Why does the submission-ingestion idempotency key need to be rescoped from the raw `submission_id` alone to `(org_id, submission_id)` once Coastal Underwriters onboards?
questions.explanation: This directly reuses the multi-tenant curriculum's idempotency-key scoping argument: an event-ID-only key becomes insufficient once multiple tenants' independent systems can generate the same raw identifier.

options.optionText: BrokerLink stopped generating submission IDs entirely after Coastal onboarded

Two tenants' independently-operated BrokerLink instances can plausibly generate the same raw identifier, and an unscoped key risks one tenant's submission silently colliding with and being dropped in favor of another's
The idempotency key was never actually necessary and could be removed once RLS was in place
Rescoping is required by BrokerLink's own API contract, unrelated to multi-tenancy

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why did the pre-call guardrail flag and log the injection-style cover letter but still let the submission proceed through the normal extraction and recommendation flow, rather than blocking it outright?
questions.explanation: This distinguishes the guardrail's audit-and-visibility role from the recommend-worker's structural no-auto-bind enforcement — both layers exist, but they don't need to duplicate each other's job.

options.optionText: The guardrail pipeline was misconfigured and should have blocked the submission

The actual bind decision was already going to pass through the human-approval gate regardless of what the cover letter requested, so the guardrail's role here is visibility and audit rather than a second blocking mechanism duplicating the gate
Guardrails are only designed to catch PII, not injection attempts
Blocking a submission outright is technically impossible once it reaches the pre-call layer

questions.questionText: What specific risk does the four-hour SLA escalation rule for the human-approval gate convert, according to the lesson?
questions.explanation: This reuses the multi-agent curriculum's escalation-design reasoning: waiting indefinitely for a human is itself a failure mode, and an SLA-bound escalation rule bounds that risk.

options.optionText: It converts a schema-validation failure into a business-rule failure
It converts an open-ended wait for a human reviewer, who could be away or backlogged indefinitely, into a bounded one with a defined fallback reviewer
It converts a low-stakes recommendation into a high-stakes one
It converts a managed guardrail service into a self-hosted one

questions.questionText: Why does the observability dashboard track the full distribution of recommend-worker iteration counts, not just the average?
questions.explanation: This reuses the agentic-systems curriculum's aggregate-observability reasoning directly: a distribution catches systemic drift an average would smooth over and hide.

options.optionText: Averages are computationally more expensive to calculate than distributions
A distribution surfaces runs quietly creeping toward the iteration cap, which often precedes an outright cap-triggered failure by days, a signal an average alone would mask
Distributions are required for regulatory compliance in insurance-adjacent AI systems
The average iteration count is always identical to the distribution's median in practice

questions.questionText: In the scenario, how was the shared-queue starvation incident caught before any underwriter filed a complaint?
questions.explanation: This is the proactive, aggregate-observability payoff the lesson describes: a dashboard signal caught the regression before it became a stack of individually-reported incidents.

options.optionText: General counsel personally noticed the delay during a routine review
The cost-and-latency dashboard flagged a queue-depth spike within minutes, surfacing the regression proactively as a graph trending the wrong way rather than waiting for a customer-reported symptom
Coastal Underwriters' own engineering team reported the issue directly to Meridian
The SLA escalation rule for the human-approval gate detected the queue backlog automatically

questions.questionText: Why does the FDE build the RAGAS eval dataset with two of Meridian's senior underwriters verifying gold answers, rather than writing the questions independently?
questions.explanation: This reuses the RAG-evaluation curriculum's exact claim about eval-dataset quality: a domain expert's verified questions and gold answers are more representative than what an FDE would write alone.

options.optionText: Meridian's contract requires underwriter sign-off on all technical artifacts
An eval set an FDE writes alone tends to be easier and less representative of how underwriters actually phrase a guideline question than a domain expert's real usage
RAGAS technically cannot score a dataset unless a domain expert authored every question
Underwriters are the only people permitted to access the underwriting guideline documents

questions.questionText: What specifically did the versioned, gated eval set catch when the FDE tuned the guideline-chunking strategy for newly added state-specific endorsement documents?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the RAG-evaluation curriculum's core CI-gate payoff: a metric regression caught automatically before a change ships, rather than surfacing later as an unattributed complaint.

options.optionText: A missing field in the recommend-worker's JSON schema
A context-recall drop on general-liability questions, flagged before the chunking change shipped rather than discovered later as a vague complaint about degraded answers
An expired OAuth token on the AtlasConnector
A cross-tenant data leak between Meridian and Coastal Underwriters

questions.questionText: Why does the FDE document the prompt-injection test against the ACORD remarks field as a "confirmed pass" rather than simply moving on once the gate held?
questions.explanation: This matches the agentic-systems curriculum's red-team standard: distinguishing a genuine exploit from an attempt the system's gates correctly blocked is itself the point of the exercise, not a formality.

options.optionText: A confirmed pass has no evidentiary value and is recorded only for completeness

The lesson's discipline is confirming gates hold under a deliberate adversarial attempt rather than assuming they do because routine traffic never broke them, and a confirmed pass is itself evidence worth recording
General counsel requires every red-team attempt, regardless of outcome, to be documented for legal reasons unrelated to the test's result
Confirmed passes are recorded only when the tool-misuse test also passes in the same session

questions.questionText: How did the FDE root-cause the partial-failure integration incident (submission marked approved in SubmissionIQ, but no corresponding Atlas exposure update) without being told in advance what had gone wrong?
questions.explanation: This is the integration curriculum's distributed-tracing discipline applied directly: one propagated trace ID makes a multi-system failure's exact point of breakdown visible without manually correlating separate systems' logs.

options.optionText: By manually re-running the entire submission pipeline from scratch until the failure reproduced
By pulling the trace ID propagated from the original BrokerLink webhook and following it through extraction, the human-approval event, and the timed-out Atlas write as one connected view
By asking Sandra Voss which system she believed was at fault
By assuming the failure was a schema-drift event without checking any evidence first

questions.questionText: Why does this sprint check every red-team finding and diagnosed integration failure against Sprint 1's original risk register, rather than treating each finding as an isolated fix to apply and move on from?
questions.explanation: This closes the loop the capstone opened in Sprint 1: reconciling findings against the original risk register is what keeps the engagement's documented risk posture honest as real evidence accumulates.

options.optionText: The risk register is a legal document that must be formally closed before any code can ship

A finding that maps to an existing register entry shows whether that risk's mitigation held or needs revising, and a finding with no corresponding entry is new information Sandra and Derek need before go-live, not a surprise to quietly patch and leave undocumented
Checking against the register is only required for findings related to tenant isolation
The risk register automatically updates itself based on red-team results with no manual review needed

questions.questionText: The Suggested Extension asks for a status-update-style summary for Sandra and Derek. What structure does the lesson say this summary should follow?
questions.explanation: This ties Sprint 4's findings back to the stakeholder-communication discipline from earlier in the curriculum — the same fixed order (what changed, what's blocked, what's needed, what's next) applies to closing out the capstone's final technical sprint.

options.optionText: A chronological narrative of every action the FDE took during the sprint, in the order it happened
What was tested, what's fixed, what's still needed, and what's next — the same order the stakeholder-communication curriculum taught for a customer-facing status update
A purely technical appendix with no summary framing at all, since Sandra and Derek are not engineers
A single sentence stating only whether the system passed or failed the red-team exercise overall

questions.questionText: Per the lesson, what distinguishes correctly parking a stakeholder's question from either dropping it or derailing the demo to answer it immediately?
questions.explanation: The scenario's Priya example shows the pattern: an explicit commitment to return, followed by an actual, on-schedule return — not silence and not an interruption of the current thread.

options.optionText: Parking means telling the stakeholder their question is not important enough to answer
Parking states explicitly that a real answer is coming and names when, then actually returns to it before the session ends, rather than silently letting it disappear
Parking means answering every question the instant it is asked, regardless of the room's current focus
Parking is only appropriate for the business sponsor's questions, never for technical or security ones

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why is answering Dev's cross-tenant question with only the latency justification for the async worker (Meridith's answer) considered non-responsive, even though it is a true fact about the same worker?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's central register-mismatch failure mode: a true fact about the right subsystem still fails to answer the question if it addresses the wrong aspect of that subsystem.

options.optionText: Latency numbers are never appropriate to share with any stakeholder on a panel

Dev asked about the control that prevents cross-tenant data leakage, not about why the step is asynchronous — the latency justification doesn't address what was actually asked, even though both concern the same worker
Dev's question was really about cost, not security, so neither answer was relevant
The async boundary itself is the vulnerability Dev was worried about

questions.questionText: What makes the FDE's answer to Dev credible beyond simply stating that tenant isolation exists?
questions.explanation: Citing a specific verification event (the red-team attempt and its confirmed refusal) is what turns the claim from an assertion into evidence, consistent with the accuracy-skepticism discipline from the earlier demo-storytelling lesson.

options.optionText: The FDE promises to add tenant isolation before the system goes live
The answer cites that Sprint 4's red-team exercise specifically attempted a cross-tenant read against the worker and confirmed it was refused — a verified result, not a design claim
The FDE shows Dev the source code for the worker during the demo
The FDE tells Dev that no client has ever reported a data leak before

questions.questionText: Why does Practice Loop step 4 specifically require the business sponsor's timeline-and-cost answer to make sense without any of the technical or security context?
questions.explanation: A sponsor's cost/timeline question answered inside a technical thread risks the same mismatch the lesson calls out for the security stakeholder — the right fact, delivered in the wrong register, reads as non-responsive.

options.optionText: Because business sponsors are not permitted to hear any technical detail during a demo

Because folding a business answer into a technical thread risks losing the sponsor's actual question inside context they don't need, the same register-mismatch risk the lesson warns against for the security stakeholder
Because the technical and security answers are always wrong if not reviewed by the business sponsor first
Because a standalone answer takes less time to prepare than an integrated one

questions.questionText: What does counting how many of three rapid-fire stakeholder questions get a real answer versus get explicitly parked (Practice Loop step 3) demonstrate that a general "practice staying calm under pressure" instruction would not?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's diagnostic step: it turns "handle pressure well" into a specific, countable check on whether parking was explicit and honored, mirroring this curriculum's consistent preference for measurable practice steps over vague reflection.

options.optionText: How fast the FDE can speak during a demo
A concrete, countable measure of triage discipline under simultaneous pressure — whether parked questions are actually explicit and actually returned to, not just a vague sense of "handling it well"
Whether the demo software can handle three simultaneous browser tabs
How many stakeholders attended the demo in total

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist the spine fact be stated "precisely enough that it cannot be phrased two contradictory ways," rather than simply being a true statement?
questions.explanation: Truth alone doesn't prevent apparent contradiction — a loosely worded true fact can still be phrased two different, seemingly conflicting ways; precision is what closes that gap.

options.optionText: Precision is a general communication virtue with no specific connection to the panel setting

A true but loosely worded fact can still be framed in two ways that sound contradictory to a panel comparing notes afterward — precision is what prevents the technical and security framings from drifting into apparent disagreement
Imprecise statements are always factually incorrect

questions.questionText: What is the Suggested Extension (adding a maintaining-team panelist) specifically asking the learner to practice, beyond the three original roles?

questions.questionText: When `routeplanner` and `fluent-bit` both mount the Pod's `request-log` `emptyDir` volume, what is actually true about what each container sees?
questions.explanation: The lesson states this precisely: a Pod-level volume mounted into two containers is the same underlying directory, which is the mechanism that makes the sidecar log-shipping pattern work.

options.optionText: Each container gets its own independent copy of the volume, synced periodically

Both containers are mounting the same underlying directory — a write by one is immediately visible to the other, with no network hop involved, because it is genuinely one shared directory, not two separate ones
Only the container that declares the volume first can write to it; the other can only read metadata
`emptyDir` volumes cannot be mounted into more than one container in the same Pod

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say a bare `ReplicaSet`, without a `Deployment` managing it, is a poor tool for rolling out a new application version deliberately?
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit: a ReplicaSet's job is only maintaining a count against a template, with no concept of a previous version or a controlled transition — that's exactly the gap a Deployment fills.

options.optionText: Editing a ReplicaSet's Pod template does not touch existing Pods — only newly created ones pick up the change, so there is no controlled, gradual mechanism for replacing the running version
ReplicaSets cannot run more than one replica at a time
A ReplicaSet automatically deletes all its Pods the moment its template is edited
ReplicaSets do not support readiness probes

questions.questionText: Given this `kubectl rollout status` output, what does it tell you about the current state of the Deployment?
questions.explanation: The output states explicitly that only 2 of 4 have updated and the progress deadline was exceeded — a stalled, incomplete rollout, not a successful or intentional partial state.

options.optionText: The rollout is stalled — only 2 of 4 replicas have successfully transitioned to the new revision, and the Deployment has exceeded its configured progress deadline without completing
The rollout has completed successfully with 2 replicas remaining on the old version by design
The Deployment has been deleted and needs to be recreated
All 4 replicas are running the new revision, but 2 have failed their liveness probes

questions.questionText: What does `kubectl rollout undo` actually do mechanically, per the lesson?
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that rollback is not a special-cased operation — it's the same scale-up/scale-down mechanism as a forward rollout, applied to the previous ReplicaSet.

options.optionText: It deletes the Deployment and recreates it from a backup snapshot
It scales a previous, retained ReplicaSet back up and the current one down — the exact same mechanism as a forward rollout, run in reverse
It reverts every Pod's container image individually, in place, without touching any ReplicaSet
It requires the original manifest file to be reapplied manually before it can proceed

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, what determines whether the Deployment controller considers a new Pod during a rollout "successfully updated"?
questions.explanation: The lesson states rollout health is judged by readiness-probe success, not merely by containers starting — this is why a `CrashLoopBackOff` Pod correctly stalls the rollout instead of being counted as done.

options.optionText: The new container process starting, regardless of application-level health
The new Pod actually passing its readiness probe, not merely its container starting
The Pod being scheduled to a node, regardless of its running state
A fixed timer elapsing after the container image is pulled

questions.questionText: The lesson states a sidecar adding 100Mi of memory per replica means a 20-replica Deployment needs 2Gi more memory purely for sidecars. Why does the lesson also say a rollout of that same Deployment needs proportionally more capacity headroom during the surge window?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is that the sidecar's footprint multiplies across every Pod the ReplicaSet creates, including temporary surge Pods during a rollout, not just the steady-state replica count.

options.optionText: Each `maxSurge` Pod created during the rollout also carries the sidecar, so the extra memory requirement applies to every surge Pod as well as every steady-state replica, not just the base 20
`maxSurge` Pods never include sidecar containers, so no additional headroom is actually needed
Sidecars are only instantiated after a rollout completes, so they don't affect surge capacity
The sidecar's memory requirement only applies once, regardless of replica or surge count

questions.questionText: Given this `kubectl rollout history` output, what does revision 1 represent, and why is it still available to roll back to even though revision 2 is the currently deployed version?
questions.explanation: The lesson states directly that old ReplicaSets are kept, scaled to zero, as revision history — this retained state is what rollback actually operates on, not just a log entry.

options.optionText: Revision 1 is the previous, working ReplicaSet and Pod template; the Deployment keeps every old ReplicaSet it created around, scaled to zero, specifically as revision history, which is what makes rolling back to it possible
Revision 1 is a snapshot of the entire cluster state, unrelated to `routeplanner` specifically
Revision numbers are cosmetic labels with no connection to any retained ReplicaSet
Revision 1 no longer exists once revision 2 is deployed; the history is purely a log with nothing to roll back to

questions.questionText: In the Practical Backend Scenario, why did the FDE use `kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=1` rather than manually reapplying the previous manifest file to fix the stalled rollout?
questions.explanation: The scenario's point is precision and speed — the retained ReplicaSet removes any need to guess or reconstruct the previous state by hand, and the mechanism is identical to a normal rollout.

options.optionText: Manually reapplying a manifest is technically impossible once a rollout has started

`rollout undo` operates on the exact retained ReplicaSet from revision 1, removing any risk of guessing the wrong image tag or reconstructing a manifest from memory, and uses the same well-understood scale-up/scale-down mechanism as any other rollout
Reapplying an old manifest would delete the Deployment object entirely
`kubectl apply` cannot be used more than twice on the same Deployment

questions.questionText: In the lesson's `routeplanner-service.yaml`, what determines which Pods this Service sends traffic to?
questions.explanation: Label selection, not naming or namespace alone, is what ties a Service to its backing Pods — this is also why two different Deployments' Pods could be accidentally included if they share a label.

options.optionText: The `metadata.name` field must exactly match the Deployment's name
The `spec.selector` field (`app: routeplanner`) — any ready Pod carrying that label is included as a traffic target, regardless of which Deployment or ReplicaSet created it
The `targetPort` value, which must be unique across the cluster
The namespace alone; all Pods in `default` receive traffic from this Service

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson call `NodePort` "almost always the wrong production choice" for exposing a service externally?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific objection is about bypassing centralized routing/TLS and coupling to volatile node IPs, not about NodePort being unreachable.

options.optionText: NodePort Services cannot be reached from outside the cluster under any configuration

It bypasses any central routing, TLS termination, or path-based rule, and ties external reachability directly to node IPs, which can change — an Ingress with a single controller is the better entry point for HTTP(S) traffic
NodePort only works with the `LoadBalancer` Service type as a prerequisite
NodePort Services do not support DNS resolution inside the cluster

questions.questionText: What specific problem does the lesson say makes `LoadBalancer` Services unwieldy once a cluster has several externally-facing services, and how does `Ingress` solve it?
questions.explanation: The lesson names the per-Service cost explicitly and contrasts it with Ingress's single-entry-point, multi-backend routing model.

options.optionText: LoadBalancer Services cannot terminate TLS, while Ingress always can

A `LoadBalancer` Service provisions one cloud load balancer per Service; an `Ingress` lets a single controller handle TLS termination and path/host-based routing to multiple backend Services behind one externally-facing load balancer
LoadBalancer Services are deprecated in current Kubernetes versions
Ingress objects replace the need for any Service object at all

questions.questionText: Why did the FDE add a second `Ingress` path rule rather than changing the `routeplanner` Service's type to `LoadBalancer` to expose the partner-facing route-history endpoint?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is about surface minimization — a path-scoped Ingress rule opens exactly what's needed, while flipping the Service type would have opened the whole Service.

options.optionText: `LoadBalancer` Services cannot be created in the `default` namespace

Changing the Service type to `LoadBalancer` would expose every port the Service defines, not just the one intended route; a scoped `Ingress` path exposes only the specific endpoint needed, through the existing TLS-terminating entry point
`Ingress` objects are required before a Service can have more than one port
The partner company's network could not reach a `LoadBalancer`-type Service under any circumstances

questions.questionText: What does CoreDNS resolve `routeplanner.default.svc.cluster.local` to?
questions.explanation: DNS resolves to the Service's stable virtual IP; the actual load-balancing across ready Pod IPs happens at the kube-proxy layer, a separate step from name resolution.

options.optionText: The IP address of whichever Pod most recently started
The Service's stable virtual IP, which `kube-proxy` (or the CNI's equivalent) then load-balances across the real Pod IPs currently marked ready in the Endpoints object
A random Pod IP chosen fresh for every DNS lookup, bypassing the Service entirely
The node IP of whichever node the Deployment happens to be scheduled on

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say a Pod's own IP address is "worthless as a stable target"?
questions.explanation: This connects directly to Phase 21's Pod-disposability lesson — the churn in Pod identity is exactly the problem a Service's stable virtual IP and DNS name exist to solve.

options.optionText: Pod IPs are randomized on every network request

Pods are disposable and routinely replaced (by rolling updates, rescheduling, or crashes), each time getting a new IP, so anything hardcoding a specific Pod IP breaks the next time that Pod is replaced
Pod IPs are not routable outside the node they run on
Only Services have IP addresses; Pods do not receive one individually

questions.questionText: The lesson opens by distinguishing itself from Module 4's "Kubernetes Networking, Security & GPU Workloads" lesson. What is that distinction?
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening paragraph states this explicitly — the difference is mechanism-and-construction versus already-running-cluster security operations.

options.optionText: Module 4's lesson does not cover Kubernetes at all; it is purely about AWS VPC design

Module 4's lesson assumes a Service already exists and focuses on securing an already-running cluster with `NetworkPolicy`; this lesson covers the earlier, more mechanism-focused question of how a Service and Ingress actually get built and how DNS/endpoint routing works
This lesson covers only `NodePort` Services, while Module 4 covers only `ClusterIP`
The two lessons cover identical content and either can be skipped

questions.questionText: What is the core difference between what the HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes and what the Cluster Autoscaler changes?
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that both HPA and VPA operate at the Pod level and never change node count — that is specifically the Cluster Autoscaler's (or Karpenter's) job.

options.optionText: HPA changes how many Pod replicas a Deployment runs; Cluster Autoscaler changes how many nodes exist in the cluster — HPA never adds node capacity, and Cluster Autoscaler never changes Pod replica counts
They are two names for the same controller, with HPA being the older, deprecated term
HPA operates on nodes, and Cluster Autoscaler operates on individual Pods
Cluster Autoscaler only runs once per day on a schedule, while HPA runs continuously

questions.questionText: In the lesson's `routeplanner-hpa.yaml`, what does `stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300` under `behavior.scaleDown` actually do?
questions.explanation: Stabilization windows specifically target scale-down oscillation, requiring a sustained reading rather than reacting to every momentary dip.

options.optionText: It delays every scale-up decision by 300 seconds regardless of metric readings
It makes the HPA wait for a sustained low metric reading over that window before actually reducing replica count, preventing rapid oscillation from a brief dip in load
It sets the minimum number of replicas to 300
It is the maximum time a Pod is allowed to remain Pending before being evicted

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson warn against running an HPA and a VPA that both actively manage CPU on the same Deployment?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific concern is the shared dependency — HPA's utilization math depends on the same request value VPA is actively changing, creating a feedback conflict.

options.optionText: Kubernetes does not allow both controllers to be installed in the same cluster

HPA scales replica count based on utilization relative to the CPU request; if VPA is simultaneously changing that same CPU request, the two controllers' decisions can fight each other rather than converge
VPA can only manage memory, never CPU, so the conflict described is not possible
Running both always causes the Deployment to be deleted automatically

questions.questionText: What does the lesson say Karpenter does differently from Cluster Autoscaler when provisioning new node capacity?
questions.explanation: The lesson names this exact distinction — skipping the node-group abstraction for direct, requirement-driven, right-sized provisioning.

options.optionText: Karpenter only works with spot instances, never on-demand capacity

Karpenter skips the pre-defined node-group abstraction and provisions right-sized nodes directly from a flexible instance-type pool based on the actual pending Pods' requirements, rather than scaling a group of identically-shaped nodes
Karpenter operates entirely at the Pod level and never adds node capacity, unlike Cluster Autoscaler
Karpenter requires the VPA to be disabled before it can run

questions.questionText: In the Practical Backend Scenario, the FDE reduces `routeplanner`'s CPU request from 500m to 200m, not to the observed average of roughly 120m. What is the reasoning?
questions.explanation: Right-sizing means leaving deliberate headroom above the observed average, not matching it exactly — matching the exact average would leave no margin for normal fluctuation.

options.optionText: Kubernetes requires CPU requests to be set in increments of 100m

Setting the request to exactly the observed average leaves no headroom for normal variance above that average, which would cause CPU throttling or scheduling pressure; 200m preserves some margin while still being far more accurate than the original 500m
200m is the minimum CPU request Kubernetes allows for any container
The VPA tool automatically overrides any value below 200m

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, what trade-off do all four scaling layers (HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter) share?
questions.explanation: The lesson closes on this exact generalization — headroom versus reactive provisioning is the same cost/latency trade-off at every layer, just at different timescales (seconds for Pods, minutes for nodes).

options.optionText: Pre-provisioned headroom costs money continuously but responds instantly; purely reactive provisioning costs nothing when idle but introduces a real, measurable delay before capacity actually exists
All four layers have identical response times regardless of provisioning strategy
Only HPA has a cost trade-off; the other three are always free to operate
The trade-off is unique to Karpenter and does not apply to Cluster Autoscaler

questions.questionText: The lesson notes Pod scheduling happens "in seconds" while new node provisioning takes "minutes." Why does this timing gap matter for how an FDE should read a scaling incident?
questions.explanation: Recognizing this timing gap as expected (not a bug) is exactly what let the FDE in the scenario correctly diagnose the Pending Pods as a capacity-provisioning delay rather than an HPA malfunction.

options.optionText: It doesn't matter; both operations always complete within the same time window

A correctly-functioning HPA can add replicas within seconds, but if those replicas need a new node, the workload will still show `Pending` Pods for several minutes even though nothing is actually broken — the gap is expected latency, not a failure
It means Cluster Autoscaler should always be disabled in favor of pre-provisioning all node capacity permanently
It implies HPA should be configured with a longer stabilization window to match node provisioning time

questions.questionText: In the lesson's two-policy YAML, what traffic does the `routeplanner-allow-db-and-redis` policy permit, given that `default-deny-all` is also applied to the same namespace?
questions.explanation: This is an egress-only allow rule scoped to two specific destination labels and ports; the default-deny policy still blocks everything not explicitly named here, including ingress.

options.optionText: Pods labeled `app: routeplanner` may make outbound (egress) connections only to Pods labeled `app: postgres` on port 5432 and Pods labeled `app: redis` on port 6379 — every other egress path stays blocked by the default-deny policy
All Pods in the namespace may reach Postgres and Redis on any port
`routeplanner` Pods may accept inbound connections from Postgres and Redis, but cannot initiate any connection themselves
The policy grants unrestricted egress to `routeplanner` Pods, overriding the default-deny policy entirely

questions.questionText: What is the difference the lesson draws between exceeding a container's CPU limit and exceeding its memory limit?
questions.explanation: The lesson calls this out explicitly as an asymmetry worth knowing — throttling versus a hard kill are very different failure signatures to debug.

options.optionText: Both result in the container being immediately killed and restarted
Exceeding a CPU limit throttles the process (it slows down but keeps running); exceeding a memory limit gets the container hard-killed (`OOMKilled`) immediately
CPU limits are enforced by the scheduler, while memory limits are enforced by the NetworkPolicy controller

questions.questionText: The lesson warns that a policy using `podSelector: {}` at the allow-rule level (matching any Pod in the namespace) rather than a specific label is a real risk. What specifically does this risk?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is specifically about future, unrelated workloads silently inheriting broad access — a scope error that isn't obvious at write-time and doesn't surface until something new is deployed into the same namespace.

options.optionText: The policy would fail to apply at all, since Kubernetes rejects empty selectors on allow rules

Every newly-scaled replica of some other, unrelated future workload placed in the same namespace would silently inherit the access the sloppy rule granted, since nobody re-reads the policy's scope every time a new Deployment appears
It would cause the NetworkPolicy to apply only to the `routeplanner` Deployment specifically and no other workload
It would prevent `routeplanner` itself from communicating with Postgres or Redis

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, what does the Kubernetes scheduler use a Pod's `resources.requests` value for?
questions.explanation: Requests are a scheduling input, distinct from limits (an enforcement ceiling) — the lesson ties this directly back to Lesson 14's HPA/Cluster-Autoscaler dependency on requests being set honestly.

options.optionText: To enforce a hard ceiling on how much CPU or memory the container may ever consume

To decide whether a node has enough allocatable capacity for a new Pod before scheduling it there — an over-packed node (from requests set too low) risks not sustaining every scheduled Pod under real load
To determine which NetworkPolicy rules apply to the Pod
To set the container's process priority relative to other containers on the same node

questions.questionText: Why did the FDE re-run the connectivity test against all 9 replicas after scaling up, rather than trusting that the policy's correctness on the original 3 replicas would hold?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's explicit framing — the mechanical guarantee is real, but an FDE verifies it under real conditions rather than taking it on faith during a customer engagement.

options.optionText: NetworkPolicy rules are evaluated independently per replica and can behave inconsistently, so full re-testing is the only way to be certain

Orthogonal-in-theory (label-based rules should cover all replicas automatically) is not the same as verified-in-practice; the test exists to actually prove the blast radius held constant rather than assume it from the policy's design
Kubernetes requires a manual policy re-application after every scaling event
The original 3 replicas use a different Pod template than the 6 added during scale-up

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson's practice loop require testing both an expected-allowed connection AND an expected-forbidden connection, rather than only confirming the allowed path works?
questions.explanation: A functional test alone can't distinguish "correctly scoped" from "too permissive" — only a deliberately-forbidden path failing as expected proves the narrower claim.

options.optionText: Testing only the allowed path is sufficient; the forbidden-path test is optional

Confirming only that the allowed path works proves the policy isn't blocking too much, but says nothing about whether it's blocking too little — the forbidden-path test is what proves the blast radius is actually bounded, not just that the intended traffic still functions
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects require exactly two test cases before they can be considered valid
The forbidden-path test is only necessary when scaling beyond 5 replicas

questions.questionText: In the lesson's `routeplanner-deployer-role` manifest, what specifically is this identity NOT permitted to do?
questions.explanation: `delete` is absent from the Deployment verbs, `resourceNames` restricts the first rule to exactly `routeplanner`, and the Pod rule grants only read verbs — no write access anywhere in this Role.

options.optionText: It cannot delete the `routeplanner` Deployment, cannot touch any other Deployment by name, and has no write access to Pods at all (only read verbs)
It cannot read or watch Pods under any circumstances
It can update any Deployment in the namespace, not just `routeplanner`

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist on verifying a grant with `kubectl auth can-i --as` rather than trusting the Role/RoleBinding YAML's correctness by inspection alone?
questions.explanation: The lesson's point is about verification discipline — asking the API server the actual question rather than trusting a manual read of potentially-interacting YAML objects.

options.optionText: `kubectl auth can-i` is required before any RBAC object can be applied to the cluster

Reasoning about the final effective permission set from YAML alone becomes genuinely error-prone once multiple bindings or role aggregation are involved; asking the API server directly gives a definitive yes/no answer instead of an inference
RBAC YAML manifests do not take effect until confirmed by `kubectl auth can-i`
`kubectl auth can-i` is the only way to create a new RoleBinding

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson recommend defaulting to a `Role` over a `ClusterRole` whenever access only needs to reach one namespace?
questions.explanation: The lesson frames this as the same least-privilege discipline applied elsewhere in this pathway — matching the scope of the grant to the scope of the actual need.

options.optionText: `ClusterRole` objects are deprecated and scheduled for removal in future Kubernetes versions

A `Role`/`RoleBinding` pair grants access scoped to exactly the one namespace it's created in, while a `ClusterRole`/`ClusterRoleBinding` pair is valid cluster-wide — using the cluster-scoped option when only namespace-scoped access is needed grants more than the task requires
`Role` objects support a wider range of verbs than `ClusterRole` objects
`ClusterRole` objects cannot be bound to ServiceAccounts, only to human users

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson's Practice Loop require checking at least three `can-i` calls that should return `no`, not just confirming the intended access returns `yes`?
questions.explanation: Mirrors Lesson 15's two-part connectivity test logic — proving a boundary requires testing the negative space, not just confirming the positive case works.

options.optionText: `kubectl auth can-i` returns an error if fewer than three checks are performed in sequence

Confirming only the intended access proves the grant works, but says nothing about whether it's also granting more than intended — checking that specific unwanted verbs correctly return `no` is what actually proves the boundary is narrow, not just functional
Checking three `no` cases is a hard requirement enforced by the Kubernetes API server itself
A single `no` check is sufficient; three is only a stylistic convention with no functional purpose

questions.questionText: What does the lesson recommend for the legitimate case where an operator genuinely needs broader, emergency diagnostic access than any scoped Role provides?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly names time-boxing and automatic expiry as what distinguishes a legitimate break-glass pattern from the standing-cluster-admin anti-pattern it opened with.

options.optionText: Permanently bind that operator's identity to `cluster-admin` so the access is always available when needed

A separate, short-lived `ClusterRoleBinding` granted for the duration of the incident and explicitly revoked afterward (or an automated break-glass tool that expires the grant), never a standing binding kept "just in case"
Disable RBAC entirely for the duration of any incident investigation
Grant the operator a second, permanent ServiceAccount with unrestricted access as a backup

questions.questionText: The lesson opens by distinguishing itself from Module 4's Kubernetes security lesson. What is that distinction?
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening paragraph states this explicitly — construction-and-verification versus already-secured-cluster auditing.

options.optionText: Module 4 does not cover RBAC at all, only network policy

Module 4 assumes RBAC is already in place and audits an already-secured, shared multi-tenant cluster; this lesson covers the earlier, hands-on question of how to build a Role/RoleBinding pair from nothing and verify it rather than assume it
This lesson only applies to ClusterRole objects, while Module 4 only covers Role objects
The two lessons are functionally identical and either can be skipped without loss

questions.questionText: If a Pod's spec does not set `serviceAccountName`, which identity does it run under when calling the Kubernetes API?
questions.explanation: This is the exact fact that makes the unscoped-`default` risk real — omission, not explicit misconfiguration, is enough to inherit whatever `default` is bound to.

options.optionText: No identity; API calls from that Pod are rejected entirely
The `default` ServiceAccount of the namespace it runs in, along with whatever permissions that ServiceAccount is bound to
A randomly-generated, single-use ServiceAccount created just for that Pod
The identity of the human who last applied the Deployment manifest

questions.questionText: The lesson says the added twist in Kubernetes, compared to Phase 20's Docker Volumes lesson, is that "the node itself is disposable too." What does this mean for what "durable" has to guarantee?
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening frames this exact escalation — surviving node loss, not just container restart, is the new bar Kubernetes storage mechanisms need to clear.

options.optionText: Nothing changes; a Docker volume and a Kubernetes PersistentVolume provide identical guarantees

Durable state must survive not just a container restart, but a Pod being rescheduled onto a completely different physical node — a guarantee a single-host Docker volume, tied to one machine's disk, cannot provide on its own
Kubernetes volumes are always slower than Docker volumes because of the added node-independence requirement
"Durable" in Kubernetes only applies to ConfigMaps and Secrets, never to application data

questions.questionText: In the lesson's manifest, what happens to `/etc/secrets` inside the `routeplanner` container if the `routeplanner-db-secret` Secret's value is later rotated?
questions.explanation: The lesson states this explicitly for ConfigMap mounts and notes Secret mounts work identically — live sync subject to the kubelet's delay, not a Pod restart trigger.

options.optionText: The mount path becomes permanently unavailable until the Pod is manually deleted and recreated

The mounted file is updated to reflect the new Secret value (subject to the kubelet's sync delay), the same live-update behavior the lesson describes for ConfigMap mounts, without requiring a Pod restart
`readOnly: true` prevents the Secret from ever being updated at the API level
Kubernetes automatically restarts the container whenever a mounted Secret changes

questions.questionText: What is the practical difference between a PVC's `ReadWriteOnce` and `ReadWriteMany` access modes, and why does the lesson warn that the choice has real consequences?
questions.explanation: The lesson calls out the EBS-doesn't-support-RWX detail specifically as the kind of consequence that makes this a deliberate choice, not a default to leave unexamined.

options.optionText: `ReadWriteOnce` allows read-write mounting by only one node at a time; `ReadWriteMany` allows multiple nodes to mount the same volume simultaneously — but not every storage backend supports RWX (EBS notably doesn't), so requiring it can constrain which StorageClass a PVC can actually bind to
`ReadWriteOnce` is read-only, and `ReadWriteMany` is the only mode that permits writes at all
The two modes are functionally identical; the name only affects logging output
`ReadWriteMany` is always faster than `ReadWriteOnce` regardless of the storage backend

questions.questionText: In the Practical Backend Scenario, why did `routeplanner`'s cache survive the node drain while `test-worker`'s cache did not, given that both Pods were deleted and rescheduled?
questions.explanation: This is exactly the PVC-versus-emptyDir distinction the lesson builds toward — the scenario is a direct, concrete demonstration of the mechanism difference described in Concepts Covered.

options.optionText: `test-worker` was scheduled onto a node with less available storage capacity

`routeplanner` used a PersistentVolumeClaim, which is not deleted along with its Pod — a new Pod referencing the same PVC reattaches to the same underlying volume with data intact; `test-worker` used `emptyDir`, which is deleted the moment its Pod is removed
`routeplanner`'s Deployment had a higher priority class than `test-worker`'s
The node drain only affected `test-worker`'s node, not `routeplanner`'s

questions.questionText: What is the relationship between a `PersistentVolumeClaim` and a `PersistentVolume`, per the lesson?
questions.explanation: The lesson describes exactly this request/fulfillment relationship, including the dynamic- provisioning path via a named StorageClass like `gp3`.

options.optionText: They are the same object under two different names, used interchangeably

A PVC is a namespaced request for storage (size, access mode, optionally a StorageClass); the cluster fulfills it by binding the PVC to an actual PersistentVolume, either pre-provisioned or dynamically created on demand by the named StorageClass
A PersistentVolume is created manually for every Pod, and the PVC only exists to delete it afterward
PVCs are cluster-scoped, while PersistentVolumes are namespace-scoped

questions.questionText: The lesson states neither a `ConfigMap` nor a `Secret` mount is "meant for data the application itself writes." What is the implication of using one for that purpose anyway?
questions.explanation: The lesson's framing is about the mechanism's intended direction — data flowing in from the API server to the Pod, not data the Pod generates and needs to persist, which is what a PVC is for.

options.optionText: ConfigMaps and Secrets are meant for data handed to the application, not data the application generates — using either for application-written output misuses a mechanism designed around the API server managing the object's content, not the running container writing to it at runtime
Kubernetes physically prevents any container process from writing to a ConfigMap or Secret mount path, making the misuse impossible
There is no meaningful downside; ConfigMaps and Secrets function identically to a PersistentVolumeClaim for any purpose
Only Secrets are restricted this way; ConfigMaps may be freely written to by the application

questions.questionText: Given this output for the private-data subnet's route table, what can you conclude about its reachability from the internet?
questions.explanation: With only a local VPC route and no `0.0.0.0/0` route of any kind (IGW or NAT), there is no path for internet traffic to arrive at all — this is the route-table backstop the lesson describes.

options.optionText: No traffic from the internet can reach resources in this subnet through this route table, since the only route is to the local VPC CIDR

This output is inconclusive without also checking the subnet's NACL
